title: Plant life cycles: seven named stages, and why some plants live four months and others for centuries

summary.text: A mustard plant lives about four months, but a coconut palm lives for decades. Both pass through the same seven stages. In this lesson you will name those stages, work out how much of a life passes before the first flower, and run the Bad Year Test with a die.
summary.art: A small mustard plant with yellow flowers in a pot beside a tall coconut palm, with a short arrow under the mustard marked 4 months and a very long arrow under the palm marked 80 years.

intro.hook: Rice, wheat, ragi, moong and mustard plants all die a few months after they are sown. Mango, coconut and tamarind trees live longer than people do. Why do some plants live for one season, when other plants can live for hundreds of years?
intro.text: A short life is not a mistake, and a short-lived plant is not a weak plant. A mustard plant that dies in April has already left thousands of seeds. In this lesson you first learn the names of the seven stages that every flowering plant goes through. You see how ferns, mosses and pines make new plants without any flowers. You sort the plants in your kitchen by how long they live. Then you roll a die for twelve years of weather, in two different places. You count the seeds that a short-lived plant and a long-lived plant leave in each place.
intro.art: A kitchen shelf with jars of rice, moong and mustard on one side and a coconut, a mango and a piece of tamarind on the other, with a question mark between them.

outcomes: I can name the seven stages of a flowering plant's life cycle in order, and say what happens in each stage.
I can say how flowering plants differ from non-flowering plants, and how ferns, mosses and conifers make new plants.
I can sort plants into annuals, biennials and perennials, and give Indian examples of each.
I can compare how long different plants live, and what share of their life passes before they first flower.
I can explain why annuals leave more seeds in places that are often cleared, and perennials in places that are left alone.
I can estimate the age of a plant from a record, from tree rings or from how fast the plant grows, and say how sure I am.
I can run a test that depends on chance fairly, by using the same rolls for both plants and repeating the test.
I can give reasons for and against growing perennial crops instead of annual crops.

terms.meaning: All the stages in the life of a living being, from the start of their life until they make young of their own. Then the young go through the same stages.
terms.example: A moong seed grows into a plant, the plant flowers, and the pods hold new moong seeds.
terms.art: A circle of arrows joining a seed, a seedling, a grown plant, a flower and a pod of seeds.

terms.meaning: The first stage of a plant's life cycle. The seed takes in water, and a root and then a shoot grow out.
terms.example: Moong seeds on a wet cloth germinate in about a day.
terms.art: A moong seed with a split coat and a short white root.

terms.meaning: The stage in which a plant becomes bigger and makes more roots, stems and leaves. The leaves make the plant's food from light, air and water.
terms.example: A mustard seedling grows from 2 leaves to a plant as tall as your knee in about five weeks.
terms.art: Three drawings of the same plant in a row, each taller and with more leaves than the one before.

terms.meaning: The stage in which a plant makes flowers. Flowers are the parts of the plant that make seeds.
terms.example: A mustard plant opens the first yellow flowers about six weeks after sowing.
terms.art: A mustard plant with a bunch of small yellow flowers at the top of the stem.

terms.meaning: The carrying of pollen from the male part of a flower to the female part of a flower of the same kind. Insects, birds, bats or the wind carry the pollen.
terms.example: A bee who visits one pumpkin flower and then another carries pollen between them on her hairs.
terms.art: A bee dusted with yellow pollen landing on the middle of a flower.

terms.meaning: The joining of a male cell from a pollen grain with an egg cell inside the flower. A seed starts to grow only after fertilisation.
terms.example: After pollen lands on a bhindi flower, each pollen grain grows a thin tube down to an egg cell.
terms.art: A cut-open flower with a pollen grain on top and a thin tube growing down to a small round egg cell.

terms.meaning: The stage after fertilisation. The fertilised egg cells grow into seeds, and the part of the flower around them grows into a fruit.
terms.example: A bhindi flower falls after one day, and the small green pod left behind grows longer every day.
terms.art: A faded flower with a small green pod swelling at its base.

terms.meaning: The carrying of seeds away from the parent plant by wind, water, animals or a bursting pod.
terms.example: A ripe mustard pod splits when dry and throws the seeds a short way.
terms.art: A dry pod splitting open with small round seeds flying out.

terms.meaning: A plant that makes flowers, and makes seeds inside a fruit.
terms.example: Mango, paddy, grass, rose, coconut and mustard are all flowering plants.
terms.art: A mango tree, a paddy plant and a rose bush, each with their flowers shown in a small circle.

terms.meaning: A plant that never makes a flower or a fruit. Ferns and mosses make spores. Conifers make seeds on cones.
terms.example: A fern on a wet wall, a cushion of moss and a pine tree are non-flowering plants.
terms.art: A fern, a patch of moss and a pine tree with cones, side by side.

terms.meaning: A single cell, far too small to see alone, that can grow into a new fern or moss. A spore holds no young plant and almost no food.
terms.example: The brown dots under a fern leaf are cases full of spores.
terms.art: The underside of a fern leaf with rows of brown dots, and fine dust falling from them.

terms.meaning: The part of a conifer that makes pollen or seeds. The seeds lie on the scales of a woody cone, with no fruit around them.
terms.example: A chir pine cone from the Himalaya holds two winged seeds on each scale.
terms.art: A woody pine cone with open scales and a winged seed lying on one scale.

terms.meaning: A plant that goes through the whole life cycle within one year or one growing season, and then dies.
terms.example: Paddy, wheat, ragi, moong, mustard, sunflower and marigold are annuals.
terms.art: A paddy plant drawn four times along a line of months: seedling, green plant, plant with grain, dry straw.

terms.meaning: A plant that takes two years. In the first year the plant grows leaves and stores food. In the second year the plant flowers, makes seeds and dies.
terms.example: A carrot stores food in the root in year one. If left in cool ground, the plant flowers in year two.
terms.art: A carrot with leaves in year one, and the same carrot with a tall flowering stalk in year two.

terms.meaning: A plant that lives for more than two years. Most perennials flower many times.
terms.example: Mango, coconut, neem, tamarind, banyan, tea and curry leaf plants are perennials.
terms.art: A mango tree shown in flower three times along a line of years.

terms.meaning: The length of time from the start of a living being's life to their death.
terms.example: A moong plant has a lifespan of about 3 months. A coconut palm has a lifespan of about 80 years.
terms.art: A short bar and a very long bar on one time line, labelled moong and coconut.

terms.meaning: The age at which a plant flowers for the first time. Before that age, the plant only grows.
terms.example: A mustard plant first flowers at about 6 weeks. A coconut palm first flowers at about 8 years.
terms.art: A time line with a seedling at the start and a small flower marking the point where flowering begins.

terms.meaning: One full round of a life cycle, from a seed to the seeds that the grown plant makes.
terms.example: Mustard can pass through three generations in one year, if there is water. A coconut palm takes about eight years for one.
terms.art: Three small plants in a row joined by arrows, each grown from a seed of the one before.

terms.meaning: An event that clears the plants from a piece of ground. Floods, fire, landslides, ploughing and digging are disturbances.
terms.example: A river in flood strips the plants from the bank. A plough clears a field before every crop.
terms.art: A bare, freshly ploughed field beside an old grove of trees.

terms.meaning: A choice in which having more of one thing means having less of another.
terms.example: A plant has only so much food. Food spent on seeds this year cannot be spent on roots and wood for next year.
terms.art: A balance with a heap of seeds on one pan and a thick root and woody stem on the other.

explanations.concept: The seven stages of a flowering plant's life cycle
explanations.definition: A life cycle is all the stages from the start of a life until that living being makes young. A flowering plant goes through seven stages, always in the same order.
explanations.description: The first stage is germination: the seed takes in water, and a root and a shoot grow out. The second is growth: the plant makes roots, stems and leaves, and the leaves make food. The third is flowering. The fourth is pollination: pollen is carried from the male part of a flower to the female part. The fifth is fertilisation: a male cell from the pollen joins an egg cell inside the flower. The sixth is fruit and seed formation: each fertilised egg cell grows into a seed, and a fruit grows around the seeds. The seventh is seed dispersal: the seeds are carried away from the parent plant. Then a seed germinates, and the stages begin again. If any one stage fails, no new seeds are made. Pollination and fertilisation are different stages. Pollination brings the pollen to the flower. Fertilisation happens afterwards, inside the flower, where nobody can see.
examples: Bhindi: the seed germinates in about a week. The plant flowers after about six weeks, and each flower lasts one day.
Mango: bees and flies pollinate the tiny flowers in spring. The fruit and the big seed form over about four months.
Paddy: wind carries the pollen. Each fertilised flower forms one grain, which is a fruit with one seed inside.
explanations.art: A circle of seven numbered pictures of a bhindi plant: a germinating seed, a leafy plant, a yellow flower, a bee on the flower, a cut flower showing a pollen tube, a green pod, and a dry pod dropping seeds.

explanations.concept: Flowering and non-flowering plants: the same round without flowers
explanations.definition: Flowering plants make seeds inside fruits. Non-flowering plants make new plants without any flower or fruit. Ferns and mosses use spores, and conifers make seeds on cones.
explanations.description: Most plants around us are flowering plants. Grass, paddy, coconut and banyan all flower, even when the flowers are small and green. Ferns never flower. Under a fern leaf are brown dots, which are cases of spores. A spore is one cell with no young plant inside and almost no food. A spore that lands on a damp spot grows into a flat green plant smaller than a fingernail. Male cells swim across that tiny plant through a film of water to reach an egg cell. From the fertilised egg cell the leafy fern grows. So a fern still has germination, growth, fertilisation and dispersal. The stages a fern does not have are flowering, pollination and fruit formation. Mosses also use spores, which form in small capsules on thin stalks. Conifers, such as pine and deodar, make pollen in small cones. Wind carries the pollen to bigger seed cones. The seeds form on the cone scales, with no fruit around them.
examples: Chir pine and deodar in the Himalaya are conifers. A chir pine cone takes about two years to ripen.
Ferns grow on wet walls, wells and tree trunks all over Kerala, the Nilgiris and Meghalaya.
Moss forms green cushions on shaded, damp bricks during the monsoon.
explanations.art: Three small cycles side by side: a bean plant with flower and pod, a pine with pollen cone and seed cone, and a fern with spores and a tiny heart-shaped plant.

explanations.concept: Annual, biennial and perennial: three lengths of life
explanations.definition: An annual lives for one growing season. A biennial lives for two years and flowers in the second. A perennial lives for more than two years.
explanations.description: The names come from the Latin word for year. An annual germinates, grows, flowers, makes seeds and dies within one year, often within three or four months. When the parent dies, only the seeds are alive. A biennial spends the first year growing leaves and storing food in a thick root or a bulb. In the second year the plant uses that food to flower, and then dies. A perennial lives on after making seeds. Some perennials are trees with wood. Others are soft plants that die back to the ground in the dry season and grow again from roots or underground stems. A woody stem is a good sign of a perennial, but it is not a sure test. Banana and ginger have no wood, and both are perennials. The same kind of plant can also live differently in different places. A chilli plant often dies in a cold winter, but lives for several years in a warm place.
examples: Annuals: paddy, wheat, ragi, bajra, moong, mustard, groundnut, sunflower, marigold.
Biennials: carrot, beetroot, cabbage and onion, when they are left to flower in cool places.
Perennials: mango, coconut, jackfruit, tamarind, neem, tea, coffee, pepper vine, banana, ginger, grass in a lawn.
explanations.art: Three time lines one above the other: a paddy plant living four months, a carrot living two years, and a mango tree with a line that runs off the page.

explanations.concept: First flowering age, and flowering once or many times
explanations.definition: The first flowering age is how old a plant is at the first flowering. Some plants flower once and die. Others flower again and again.
explanations.description: Every plant grows for a while before flowering. A mustard plant lives about 120 days and first flowers at about day 40. So one third of the life passes before the first flower. A coconut palm lives about 80 years and first flowers at about 8 years, which is one tenth of the life. A mango tree grown from a seed first flowers at about 5 years. That tree can live 100 years, so one twentieth of the life passes first. All annuals and biennials flower in one season and then die. Most perennials flower many times. A few perennials grow for many years, flower only once and then die. Neelakurinji, a shrub of the Palani and Munnar hills, grows for 12 years. Then all the shrubs on a hillside flower together, make seeds and die. The talipot palm of Kerala and Sri Lanka grows for many decades, often put at 30 to 80 years, and flowers once. A plant that flowers once can put all the stored food into one very large seed crop.
examples: Mustard: first flower at about 40 days, in a life of about 120 days.
Coconut palm: first flower at about 8 years, then flowers every month for about 70 years.
Neelakurinji flowered across the hills in 1994, 2006 and 2018, each time 12 years apart.
explanations.art: Four life bars of different lengths, each with a small flower marking the first flowering: mustard, coconut, mango and neelakurinji, whose only flower is at the very end.

explanations.concept: Why there are both annuals and perennials: a trade-off
explanations.definition: A plant has only so much food to spend. An annual spends nearly all of it on seeds in one season. A perennial keeps some for roots, wood and buds, so the plant can live to make seeds again.
explanations.description: Food spent on seeds cannot be spent on staying alive. This is a trade-off. An annual moves almost everything from the leaves and stem into the seeds, and the plant dies. A perennial holds food back to build wood and deep roots. So a perennial makes no seeds at all for the first years. The reward comes later. A grown tree has leaves high in the light and roots deep in the ground, so the tree can make a large seed crop every year. Which way leaves more seeds? That depends on how safe it is to be a grown plant. A seed is small, and most seedlings die. A grown tree usually lives through the next year. So where grown plants are safe, living on is the better bet. But a flood, a fire or a plough kills grown plants and takes away all the years that the perennial spent growing. An annual loses only one season, and new plants grow from seeds in the soil. The Bad Year Test in this lesson lets you count this with a die.
examples: A paddy plant ends as dry straw, with almost all the food moved into the grain.
A mango seedling makes no fruit for about five years, and then fruits for a hundred years.
In 2018, the cyclone called Gaja blew down lakhs of coconut palms in Tamil Nadu. A new palm needs about eight years to bear.
explanations.art: A balance: on one pan a small plant with a big heap of seeds, on the other a young tree with thick roots and no seeds.

explanations.concept: Where annuals live and where perennials live
explanations.definition: Annuals are most common where the ground is often cleared or where the growing season is short. Perennials are most common where plants are left alone for many years.
explanations.description: An event that clears the plants from the ground is called a disturbance. Floods, fires, landslides, ploughing and digging are disturbances. On ground that is disturbed often, such as a riverbank, a roadside or a ploughed field, most of the plants are annuals. They germinate fast, flower young and leave seeds before the next disturbance. Deserts also have many annuals. After a good rain in the Thar, small annuals germinate, flower and seed within six to eight weeks. Then they wait as seeds, sometimes for years. In an old forest the ground is rarely cleared, and almost every plant is a perennial. When a plot of land is cleared and then left alone, the plants change in a regular order. Annual weeds cover the plot in the first year. Perennial grasses and herbs follow, then shrubs, and after many years trees. Annuals are a small share of all flowering plant species, yet they cover a large part of the world's farmland.
examples: The weeds in a pavement crack or on a building site are mostly annuals.
A sacred grove, such as a kavu in Kerala or a devarakadu in Kodagu, is full of very old perennials.
A paddy field is ploughed before every crop, so farmers make a disturbance on purpose.
explanations.art: A split picture: a river sandbank with small flowering weeds on one side, and a dark old grove of big trees on the other.

explanations.concept: How long plants live: from two months to nearly five thousand years
explanations.definition: Lifespan is the time from the start of a life to death. Plant lifespans range from about two months to several thousand years.
explanations.description: Thale cress, a small weed that scientists grow in laboratories, goes from seed to seed in about two months. Moong lives about three months, mustard about four and paddy about five. A banana stem lives about one year, but new stems keep coming from the base of the clump. A coconut palm lives about 80 years. Many trees outlive every person who planted them. The Great Banyan in the botanic garden at Howrah is said to be at least 250 years old. A peepal tree at Anuradhapura in Sri Lanka was planted more than 2,200 years ago. A giant sequoia in California lived for more than 3,000 years. The oldest living single tree with a counted age is a bristlecone pine in California, at about 4,800 years. One bristlecone lifespan is as long as 14,400 mustard lifespans, one after another. The oldest trees are often small and slow-growing, and live in cold, dry places. Slow growth makes dense wood that insects and rot cannot easily enter.
examples: Thimmamma Marrimanu, a banyan in Andhra Pradesh, is said to be more than 550 years old.
Some baobab trees in Africa have been dated to more than 2,000 years.
A talipot palm lives for many decades and then dies after one flowering.
explanations.art: A long time line marked from 0 to 5,000 years, with tiny bars for moong and mustard at the start and long bars for a banyan, a peepal, a sequoia and a bristlecone pine.

explanations.concept: How we find out a plant's age
explanations.definition: A plant's age can be known from a written record, counted from growth rings in the wood, measured by carbon dating, or estimated from how fast the plant grows.
explanations.description: The surest way is a record of the planting. The peepal at Anuradhapura has a planting date in old chronicles. The second way is to count rings. In places with seasons, a tree adds one ring of wood each year. Scientists drill out a core of wood as thin as a pencil, so the tree is not cut down. Tropical trees with no clear seasons often have no clear rings. The third way is carbon dating, which measures how old a piece of wood is. Baobabs were dated this way, because old baobabs are hollow. The fourth way is to estimate from the rate of growth. A coconut palm makes about 12 to 14 leaves a year, and each fallen leaf leaves a ring-shaped scar on the trunk. So the number of scars divided by 13 gives a rough age. An estimate from a growth rate is only as good as the rate. Plants grow faster in a wet year and slower in a dry year. So an honest estimate is given as a range, such as 'between 20 and 30 years'.
examples: In 1957, cores from a bristlecone pine showed it was more than 4,600 years old.
A coconut trunk with 390 leaf scars is about 30 years old, because 390 divided by 13 is 30.
In the Leaf Clock in this lesson, you estimate the age of a potted plant from the leaves made in three weeks.
explanations.art: A scientist drilling a thin core from a tree trunk, with a close-up of the core showing many fine rings, beside a coconut trunk with ring-shaped leaf scars.

explanations.concept: How a plant passes from growth to flowering
explanations.definition: A plant flowers when a chemical signal made in the leaves reaches the buds. The leaves make the signal when the plant is big enough and the season is right.
explanations.description: Many plants tell the season by the length of the night. In 1934, James Knott covered parts of spinach plants to find which part senses this. He found that the leaves sense it, and the buds do not. In 1936, the scientist Mikhail Chailakhyan gave only the leaves of a chrysanthemum the right day length. The buds, which never had it, still made flowers. He said that a signal must travel from the leaves to the buds, and he named the signal florigen. Nobody could find florigen for seventy years. In 2007, two teams found it. Florigen is a small protein made in the leaves. The protein travels in the plant's sap to the buds, and there switches on the genes that build a flower. A young plant does not answer the season until they have grown enough leaves. So the first flowering age depends on the size of the plant and on the season together. Plants sense the season and their own size, and then flower. Some scientists describe this as a choice the plant makes, and others describe the response as automatic.
examples: Chrysanthemums flower when nights grow long, and so do many paddy varieties.
A leaf from a flowering plant, grafted onto a plant that is not flowering, can make that plant flower.
Farmers light chrysanthemum fields at night to delay the flowers until a festival.
explanations.art: A plant with one leaf under a small shade, and dotted arrows running inside the stem from that leaf up to a bud that is opening into a flower.

explanations.concept: Our food comes mostly from annuals
explanations.definition: Most of the food energy that people eat comes from annual plants, above all rice, wheat and maize. Farmers chose annuals because an annual puts a large share of the plant into seeds.
explanations.description: Look at a ripe paddy plant. About half of the dry weight of the plant above the ground is grain. No wild perennial puts that much into seeds, because a perennial keeps food back for next year. About ten thousand years ago, people began to save and sow the seeds of wild annual grasses and pulses. Each year they kept seed from the plants with the most and biggest grains. An annual also suits a ploughed field, because ploughing is a disturbance and annuals do well after one. Rice, wheat and maize together now give people about half of their food energy. Perennials feed us too. Coconut, banana, mango, jackfruit, tea, coffee, pepper and sugarcane are perennials. A perennial crop is not sown each year, and the roots hold the soil all year. But a farmer must wait some years for the first harvest. Many farmers in Kerala and Karnataka grow both together. Under coconut palms they grow banana, pepper, ginger and vegetables.
examples: A thali with rice, sambar, a vegetable and curd: the rice and the dal both come from annuals.
Coconut oil, pepper and tamarind in the same thali come from perennials.
After the cyclone of 2018, farmers in Tamil Nadu grew groundnut and banana between their new coconut seedlings.
explanations.art: A steel thali with rice and sambar, with thin lines joining each food to a small drawing of the plant: paddy, toor dal, a coconut palm, a tamarind tree, a pepper vine.

explanations.concept: Should our grain crops be perennial?
explanations.definition: Scientists agree that perennial plants hold soil better than annual crops. They disagree about whether perennial grains can feed as many people.
explanations.description: Every year, farmers plough and sow the fields of annual grain again. Bare, ploughed soil can wash away in heavy rain. A perennial grain would be sown once and harvested for years. In China, scientists at Yunnan University crossed rice with a wild perennial rice from Africa. Their perennial rice, called PR23, gave eight harvests in four years from one sowing. The yields were close to those of annual rice. In Kansas in the United States, the Land Institute breeds a perennial grass whose grain is sold as Kernza. Its roots go three metres deep. So far, its grain yield is much lower than the yield of wheat.
examples: Perennial rice PR23 has been grown by farmers in Yunnan since 2018.
Kernza grain is used in some bread and breakfast foods in the United States.
Sugarcane is a perennial grass that Indian farmers already cut and regrow for two or three years.

perspectives.who: Scientists who breed perennial grains, such as Fengyi Hu in Yunnan and the Land Institute in Kansas
perspectives.explanation: A perennial grain is sown once. The farmer saves seed, ploughing and many days of work each year. Deep roots hold the soil and find water in a dry spell. The yields can be raised by breeding, as the yields of annuals once were.

perspectives.who: Many crop scientists who work on annual grains
perspectives.explanation: A plant that saves food for next year has less to put into grain. This is the trade-off, and breeding cannot remove it fully. Weeds and diseases also build up in a field that is never ploughed. With more people to feed, lower yields would mean clearing more forest for fields.

perspectives.who: Farmers who grow annuals and perennials together
perspectives.explanation: The two can share one field. Trees and perennial crops hold the soil and give something every year. Annual grains between them give the staple food. Neither one has to do everything.

explanations.art: A split field: on one side a farmer ploughing bare soil, on the other a field of grass-like grain with very deep roots shown below the ground.

explanations.definition: Humans and other animals grow weaker with age, and this is called ageing. Scientists disagree about whether long-lived trees age in this way.
explanations.description: A tree makes new leaves, new buds and a new layer of wood every year. So the working parts of a very old tree are always young. In 2001, scientists compared bristlecone pines from 23 years old to more than 4,700 years old. The old trees made pollen and seeds as healthy as those of the young trees. In 2020, scientists in China studied ginkgo trees up to 667 years old. The growing layer under the bark showed no sign of ageing. Very old trees usually die from outside causes, such as storms, fire, drought, fungi or the axe. But old trees also carry more wounds and rot, and they must lift water higher.
examples: A bristlecone pine about 4,700 years old still made seeds that germinated well.
Old ginkgo trees kept making new wood and defence chemicals at the same rate as young ones.
An old banyan replaces a rotted trunk with new trunks that grow down from the branches.

perspectives.who: Scientists who say some trees do not age
perspectives.explanation: The growing points of an old tree work as well as those of a young tree. Nothing inside the tree sets a time limit. A tree dies when a storm, a fire, a drought or a disease kills them, and the chance of that adds up over the years.

perspectives.who: Scientists who say trees age slowly
perspectives.explanation: No tree lives for ever, and the oldest trees grow very little. Damage, rot and small errors in the cells build up with time. The tree becomes less able to survive the next storm or drought. That slow weakening is ageing, even if it takes thousands of years.

explanations.art: A very old, twisted pine with mostly bare wood and one strip of green needles and fresh cones.

explanations.concept: One life cycle, one trip round the Sun
explanations.description: An annual lives for one growing season because the Earth has seasons. The Earth's axis is tilted, so the days grow longer and shorter as the Earth goes round the Sun. In much of India the year also has one rainy season, which the monsoon brings. An annual fits a whole life into the wet or mild part of one trip round the Sun, and waits out the rest as a seed. Near the equator, where every month is warm and wet, annuals are few. Some scientists think that the first annuals arose from perennials when climates became drier or more seasonal. The same change, from perennial to annual, has happened many separate times in different plant families. Nobody has watched it happen, so this is an idea that fits the evidence. A year on Mars lasts 687 Earth days. Nobody knows how a mustard plant would time a life there.
examples: Wheat in Punjab is sown in the cool season and harvested before the hot summer.
Ragi in Karnataka is sown with the monsoon and harvested when the rains end.
In the rainforests of the Andaman Islands, almost every plant is a perennial.
explanations.art: The Earth shown at four points on a circle round the Sun, with a small annual plant drawn at each point: seed, green plant, flowering plant, dry plant with seeds.

agreed.text: Every flowering plant goes through the same stages in the same order: germination, growth, flowering, pollination, fertilisation, fruit and seed formation, and seed dispersal.
agreed.evidence: Gardeners, farmers and botanists have watched thousands of kinds of plants from seed to seed. When pollination or fertilisation is stopped in a test, no seeds form.

agreed.text: Ferns and mosses make new plants from spores, and conifers make seeds on cones. None of them ever flowers.
agreed.evidence: Spores from a fern leaf have been grown on damp soil under a microscope many times. The tiny flat plant and then the new fern can be watched.

agreed.text: Annuals put a much larger share of their body into seeds than perennials do.
agreed.evidence: Scientists dry and weigh whole plants and their seeds. About half of the dry weight of a paddy plant above the ground is grain.

agreed.text: Annuals are most common on ground that is often disturbed and in dry places with short growing seasons.
agreed.evidence: Counts of plants on cleared plots, riverbanks and fields show mostly annuals in the first years. Annuals are most common in hot, dry regions.

agreed.text: Some trees live for thousands of years.
agreed.evidence: Ring counts on cores of wood from bristlecone pines give ages of more than 4,600 years. Carbon dating of baobab wood gives more than 2,000 years for the oldest.

agreed.text: A signal made in the leaves, called florigen, tells the buds to make flowers.
agreed.evidence: Giving only the leaves the right day length makes a plant flower. In 2007 the signal was found to be a small protein that travels from leaf to bud.

challenging.claim: A plant that lives longer is a more successful plant.
challenging.for: A long-lived tree makes seeds for hundreds of years, and is still standing when short-lived plants are gone.
challenging.against: On ground that is often cleared, annuals leave more seeds than perennials. Annuals cover riverbanks, fields and deserts that most trees cannot hold.
challenging.context: This card is about the belief that a long life is always better for a plant than a short life.

challenging.claim: An annual plant dies because the plant is weak or worn out.
challenging.for: The plant turns yellow and dry soon after the seeds ripen, which looks like wearing out.
challenging.against: The plant moves the food from the leaves into the seeds, and that empties the leaves. When the flowers of a soybean plant are picked off, the plant stays green much longer.
challenging.context: This card is about why an annual plant dies after making seeds.

challenging.claim: The biggest trees are the oldest trees.
challenging.who: Many people, and many scientists before the 1950s.
challenging.for: A tree gets bigger every year, so a very big tree must have had many years to grow.
challenging.against: The oldest trees with counted ages are small bristlecone pines on dry, cold mountains. A tree in good soil can grow huge in a few hundred years.
challenging.context: This card is about whether you can tell a tree's age from the tree's size.

challenging.claim: Perennial grains could replace annual rice and wheat.
challenging.for: Perennial rice in China has given eight harvests from one sowing, with yields close to annual rice. Perennial roots hold the soil.
challenging.against: A plant that saves food for next year has less for grain. Perennial wheat-like grains still yield far less than wheat. Weeds and diseases build up in unploughed fields.
challenging.context: This card is about a real argument among crop scientists: should grain crops live for many years?

challenging.claim: Neelakurinji shrubs count twelve years before they flower.
challenging.who: Some botanists who study plants that flower together after many years.
challenging.for: Flowerings have been recorded every 12 years since 1838. Shrubs on different hills flower in the same year.
challenging.against: Nobody has found a part of the plant that counts years. Other scientists think the shrubs flower when they reach a certain size or store of food, and that the weather keeps them in step.
challenging.context: This card is about how neelakurinji shrubs, which flower once in 12 years, keep time.

big_questions.q: A mustard plant lives four months and a banyan lives five hundred years. Does the banyan have more life, or the same life spent more slowly?
big_questions.hint: Think about what each plant does in a life: germinates, grows, flowers, makes seeds. Does either one leave anything out?

big_questions.q: When an annual dies, the seeds are still alive. Has that plant's life ended?
big_questions.hint: Think about what the seed carries from the parent. Then think about what is new in the seed.

big_questions.q: In the Bad Year Test, luck decided each single year. Can something that depends on luck still follow a rule?
big_questions.hint: Think about one roll of a die and about sixty rolls of a die. Which can you predict?

big_questions.q: A farmer who plants a coconut seedling may be old before the palm is fully grown. Why do people plant trees whose fruit they may never eat?
big_questions.hint: Think about who planted the trees whose mangoes and coconuts you eat now.

big_questions.q: Almost all our staple food comes from plants that die every year. Is that a strength of our farming or a risk?
big_questions.hint: Think about what must happen every single year for an annual crop. Then think about what a storm does to a grove of trees.

big_questions.q: A bristlecone pine germinated before the pyramids of Egypt were built, and is alive today. What could a living being who is that old tell us about the Earth?
big_questions.hint: The width of each yearly ring shows whether that year was wet or dry. Scientists read old trees to learn about past weather.

how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out which trees are the oldest? This card tells the true story of Edmund Schulman and the bristlecone pines.
how_we_found_out.story: Until the 1950s, most people believed that the biggest trees were the oldest. The giant sequoias of California can be as tall as a 20-storey building or more, and stumps of cut sequoias showed more than 3,000 rings. Edmund Schulman was a scientist at the University of Arizona who studied tree rings. He wanted very old trees, because their rings record the wet and dry years of the past. He noticed that the oldest trees he found were not in rich forests. They grew slowly in dry, rocky places. In 1953 he heard of old pines high in the White Mountains of California. The trees there were short and twisted, with more bare wood than bark. Schulman drilled out thin cores of wood, which does not kill a tree, and counted the rings under a microscope. Many trees were more than 4,000 years old. In 1957 he worked out that one tree was more than 4,600 years old. That tree is now known as Methuselah. He wrote that these trees live so long because of their hard life. Slow growth makes dense wood full of resin, which insects, rot and fire cannot easily destroy.
how_we_found_out.who: Edmund Schulman, an American scientist who studied tree rings
how_we_found_out.when: Schulman first cored the bristlecone pines in 1953. He sampled Methuselah in 1957, and his account was published in 1958.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That the biggest trees, growing in the best places, are the oldest. Ring counts showed that small, slow-growing pines on dry mountains were many centuries older than the giant sequoias.
how_we_found_out.art: A man in 1950s field clothes turning a thin drill into the trunk of a short, twisted pine on a bare, rocky mountainside.

roots.context: In this lesson you named the seven stages of a plant's life, and you ran the Bad Year Test with a short-lived and a long-lived plant. Here we ask what short and long lives show about life, and about ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: In the Bad Year Test, the perennial left more seeds in the old grove, where the ground was rarely cleared. The annual left more seeds on the riverbank, where the ground was cleared often. Neither plant won in both places. So a short life suits ground that is often cleared, and a long life suits ground that is left alone.
deep_truth.habit: We rank lives by their length. We think of a tree that lives 500 years as a greater plant than a weed that lives four months. The count of seeds shows that each length of life works well in one kind of place and badly in the other.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Bad Year Test, the same die rolls decided the years for both plants. Over three runs of 12 years, the perennial usually left more seeds in the old grove, and the annual usually left more on the riverbank. In the world, annuals cover riverbanks, fields and deserts, and old forests are almost all perennials. If your own totals were different, write down what you found.

three.who_am_i: You are a long-lived animal. You will spend about one fifth of your life growing up, as a coconut palm spends one tenth. A long childhood works well for someone who is looked after and kept safe while they grow, just as a long life works well for a tree in a grove that is left alone.
three.what_is_life: Every kind of living being divides a life between growing and making young. A mustard plant and a banyan divide that time very differently, and both ways have lasted for millions of years.
three.what_is_this_world: The world is made of places that are cleared often and places that are left alone. Each kind of place is home to living beings whose length of life suits it.

roots.thread: Every flowering plant passes through the same seven stages. A mustard plant fits them into four months, and a banyan spreads them over centuries. The stages are the same, and only the timing differs. The timing suits the place: a riverbank that floods, or a grove that stands for a thousand years. Many sages taught that one life takes many forms, and that no form is higher than another.

teachings.teaching: The morning mushroom knows nothing of the evening and the dawn. The summer cicada knows nothing of spring and autumn. An ancient tree counted eight thousand years as one spring. Zhuangzi says that the short-lived cannot be measured by the long-lived.
teachings.link: Lifespans in this lesson run from two months to nearly five thousand years. Zhuangzi warns against judging one length of life by another. The Bad Year Test gives a reason from science: each length suits a different place.
verse: 朝菌不知晦朔，蟪蛄不知春秋。
楚之南有冥靈者，以五百歲爲春，五百歲爲秋。
上古有大椿者，以八千歲爲春，八千歲爲秋。

teachings.teaching: Tiruvalluvar says that doing a thing at the right time, in step with the season, is what keeps good fortune from slipping away.
teachings.link: An annual fits a whole life into one wet season, and a plant flowers when the leaves sense the right time of year. The Kural is advice for people, and science does not test advice. But plants show how much depends on timing.

teachings.teaching: The Buddha says that all things that are put together pass away. A person who sees this clearly is freed from sorrow.
teachings.link: The mustard plant ends in four months and the bristlecone pine in five thousand years, but both end. The bristlecone pine lives far longer, but its life still comes to an end.

science.text: Annuals are a small share of all kinds of flowering plants, but they are most common in hot, dry and often-disturbed places, and they cover much of the world's farmland.
The change from perennial to annual has happened many separate times in different plant families.
Some long-lived trees may not age at all, and die only from outside causes such as storms, fire and disease.

other_view.who: Many biologists who study how lifespans evolve
other_view.view: In each place, the plants whose timing left the most surviving young had the most descendants. Over many generations, that alone made annuals common on riverbanks and trees common in forests. On this view the fit between a life and a place needs no plan behind it. It is the result of counting who survived.

practice.title: Two lifespans in two hands
practice.say: Hold one mustard seed in your left hand. Put your right hand flat on something made of wood, such as a door or a table. The seed's kind lives for four months. The tree that made the wood may have lived for sixty years. Close your eyes and take five slow breaths. Feel the small seed and the hard wood. You are older than any mustard plant and younger than most trees.
practice.kid: Hold a mustard seed in one hand. Put the other hand on a wooden door. Close your eyes. Take five slow breaths. One kind lives four months. The other lived sixty years. Feel them both.

ask: A mustard plant lives four months and leaves thousands of seeds. Is that a short life or a full life?
You will take many years to grow up, as a coconut palm does. What does a long childhood give you that a mustard plant does not have?
In the Bad Year Test, no plant won in both places. Is there any way of living that is best everywhere?

story.title: Six Times Blue
story.note: Valli, Paatti, the clerk and the tahsildar are made up, and so is the scene in the office. These things are real. Neelakurinji is a shrub of the Palani hills, the Nilgiris and the Munnar hills. The shrubs grow for 12 years, flower together, make seeds and die. Flowerings have been recorded every 12 years since 1838, and the last ones were in 1994, 2006 and 2018. Elders of the Paliyan people of the Palani hills are said to have counted their ages in kurinji flowerings. Bees make honey from the flowers. The rules for an old-age pension are more complicated than in this story.
text: In August the hill behind Valli's village turned blue.

It did not happen in a day. First there were a few flowers on the bushes by the path, small and pale, like scraps of sky. Then there were more. By the end of the month the whole slope was blue from the stream to the ridge, and the bees were so loud that Valli could hear them from the doorway.
She was ten years old. For all ten years those bushes had been green and nothing else. She had walked through them every day and never once seen a bud.
Paatti stood beside her, looking up at the hill. "My sixth," she said.

Three days later they took the bus to the taluk office in Kodaikanal. Paatti's knees were bad now, and she could not climb to the honey cliffs any more. A neighbour had said there was a pension for people over sixty.
The clerk was a young man from Madurai, down in the plains. He had a form, a pen and a wall full of files. Behind his chair hung a tourism poster that nobody in the office looked at any more.
"Date of birth?" he asked.
"I do not have one," said Paatti.
"Everybody has one, Amma. I mean the paper. A birth certificate. A school record."
"I was born in the forest. Nobody wrote it down. I did not go to school."
The clerk put down his pen. "Then how do I know that you are sixty?"
"I have seen the kurinji flower six times," said Paatti. "The first time I could not walk yet. My mother carried me through the flowers on her back. She told me so."
The clerk smiled, not unkindly. "Amma, flowers come every year. I have a jasmine in a pot at home. She flowers every week. If I counted my age in jasmine flowers, I would be a thousand years old."
He slid the form back across the desk. "Bring some proof. Anything written."
They sat on the bench outside, waiting for the afternoon bus. Paatti was quiet. Valli was angry, and the anger made it hard to think.

The clerk was not stupid. He was right about his jasmine. A jasmine bush flowers, and rests, and flowers again, year after year, and the bush goes on living. The mango tree by the bus stand did the same. So did the coffee bushes and the orange trees. Every plant he knew flowered again and again.
The kurinji was a different kind of plant. Valli knew the whole of the kurinji's life, because Paatti had told her every part.

After the flowers came the seeds. After the seeds, every bush on the hill dried up and died, all in the same season. The next monsoon, the ground under the dead sticks was covered in seedlings. The seedlings grew for eleven years and made nothing but leaves. In the twelfth year, every one of them flowered together. A kurinji flowered once in a whole life, and that life was twelve years long.
So the bushes that were blue today had all germinated in the same monsoon. Their parents had flowered twelve years before, and the parents of those twelve years before that.
"Paatti," said Valli. "Give me the form."

She turned it over and borrowed a pencil from the tea seller. At the bottom she wrote this year, 2018. She took away twelve and wrote 2006 above it. Then 1994. Then 1982, 1970 and 1958. Six years, one above the other.
"In 1958 you were on your mother's back," she said. "You could not walk yet. So you were born in 1957, or the year before."
"If you say so," said Paatti. "I only know the flowers."
Valli went back in alone. The clerk looked up.
"Sir," she said. "How many years have you worked in this office?"
"Four. Why?"
"In those four years, did you ever see the hills blue, before this month?"
He thought about it. "No."

"Your jasmine flowers every week and stays alive. The kurinji grows for twelve years, flowers once, and dies. All of them together. These are the years." She put the paper on his desk. "My grandmother has seen all six. I have seen one. You have seen one as well, sir. It is outside the window."
The clerk looked at the six numbers. "A girl with a pencil is not proof either," he said. But he said it slowly.
"Then read your own wall," said Valli.
He turned in his chair. The poster behind him showed a blue hillside. He had sat under it for four years. Across the top it said: KURINJI SEASON 2018. THE FLOWER THAT BLOOMS ONCE IN TWELVE YEARS.
He read it twice. Then he picked up the paper and went into the inner room, where the tahsildar sat. Valli heard a woman's voice ask a question, and then laugh.

The tahsildar came out herself. She was a grey-haired woman with spectacles on a chain. "My father was posted here in 1970," she said. "He wrote to us that the hills had gone blue. I have the letter still." She looked at Paatti through the doorway, and at the six numbers. "The planters wrote down the flowerings long before that. It has never been eleven years, and never thirteen."
She took the clerk's pen. On the form, beside Date of birth, she wrote: About 1957. Under it she wrote: Reckoned by six flowerings of kurinji, 1958 to 2018.
On the bus home, the road ran along the blue hillside for a long way. Paatti held the stamped paper in both hands.
"He thought I was counting jasmine," she said, and laughed until she coughed.
Valli pressed her forehead to the window. By next summer these bushes would be dry sticks, and under them the seedlings would be coming up. She counted on her fingers.
"At my second blue, I will be twenty-two," she said. "At my third, thirty-four."
"And I will see my seventh," said Paatti. "I intend to. Somebody has to keep the count."
story.epiphany: For the parent: the clerk knows only plants that flower again and again, so flowers cannot be a calendar for him. Valli sees that kurinji has a different life cycle. Each shrub lives 12 years and flowers once, and all the shrubs on the hills flower together. That makes each flowering a mark 12 years from the last. Six flowerings, from 1958 to 2018, give Paatti's age.
ask: The clerk said that flowers come every year. For which plants is he right, and why is kurinji different?
Why does it matter that all the kurinji shrubs on the hill flower in the same year?
Valli wrote 2018, 2006, 1994, 1982, 1970 and 1958. How did she get from those years to about 1957?
Three things helped the clerk believe Valli: her sums, the poster and the tahsildar's letter. Which is the strongest evidence, and why?
Could you count a person's age in mango flowerings? What would you need to know first?

games.title: Where Did the Cycle Stop? Find the stage that failed
games.context: This is a card game about the seven stages of a flowering plant's life cycle. Each card tells what happened to a plant. Players decide which stage failed, so that no new seeds were made.

printables.title: 21 cycle cards: what happened on the front, the stage that failed and the reason on the back

items.f: Moong seeds lie in a dry jar for a whole year.
items.b: GERMINATION. A seed cannot start to grow without water.

items.f: Bajra seeds are sown in a field. No rain falls for two months.
items.b: GERMINATION. The seeds stay dry, so no root or shoot grows out.

items.f: A mango stone is dried on a shelf for two months. Then the stone is sown.
items.b: GERMINATION. A mango seed dies when dried, so the seed never grows.

items.f: A goat eats every tomato seedling in a pot, down to the soil.
items.b: GROWTH. The seedlings germinated, but they were eaten before they could grow up.

items.f: Sunflower seedlings come up under a table, where no light reaches them.
items.b: GROWTH. Without light the leaves cannot make food, so the seedlings stop growing and die.

items.f: Brinjal seedlings in a pot get no water after the first week.
items.b: GROWTH. A plant cannot make food or new leaves without water.

items.f: A chrysanthemum plant grows under a street lamp that shines all night.
items.b: FLOWERING. This plant flowers only when the nights are long. Under the lamp, the leaves never sense a long night.

items.f: A mango tree grown from a seed is two years old and healthy.
items.b: FLOWERING. The tree has not reached the first flowering age, which is about five years.

items.f: A gardener pinches off every bud on a rose bush before the bud can open.
items.b: FLOWERING. With no open flowers, no pollen can be given or received.

items.f: A pumpkin vine flowers on a balcony closed in by a fine net. No insect can get in.
items.b: POLLINATION. Pumpkin pollen must be carried by insects from one flower to another.

items.f: Insect spray kills all the bees in an apple orchard in the week the trees flower.
items.b: POLLINATION. The flowers open, but nobody carries the pollen between them.

items.f: A papaya tree with only female flowers stands alone. No other papaya tree grows for many kilometres.
items.b: POLLINATION. There is no pollen of the same kind to reach the flowers.

items.f: Pollen lands on tomato flowers on a day of fierce heat. The pollen dries up on the flower.
items.b: FERTILISATION. The pollen arrived, but died before a male cell could reach an egg cell.

items.f: Pollen lands on paddy flowers on a very cold night. The pollen tubes stop growing half way.
items.b: FERTILISATION. Pollination happened, but no male cell joined an egg cell.

items.f: A bee brings pollen to a bean flower. A tiny grub has already eaten the egg cells inside.
items.b: FERTILISATION. There is no egg cell for the male cell to join.

items.f: A brinjal flower is fertilised. Then the plant gets no water, and the tiny young fruit drops off.
items.b: FRUIT AND SEED FORMATION. The fruit and the seeds inside did not finish growing.

items.f: A parrot bites off the green mangoes while the seed inside is still soft.
items.b: FRUIT AND SEED FORMATION. The seeds were not yet ripe, so they cannot grow.

items.f: A farmer picks every bhindi pod while the pod is tender and the seeds are white.
items.b: FRUIT AND SEED FORMATION. The seeds were picked before they were ripe. Farmers leave a few pods to dry for seed.

items.f: Birds usually carry neem fruits away. This year every fruit falls into the deep shade under the tree.
items.b: SEED DISPERSAL. Seedlings crowded in the parent's shade get too little light and water.

items.f: A banyan tree is covered in ripe figs. All the birds and bats that eat figs have gone from the town.
items.b: SEED DISPERSAL. Nobody carries the seeds to a wall or a branch where a banyan can start.

items.f: A plant whose seeds have tiny hooks grows in a field where no animal ever walks.
items.b: SEED DISPERSAL. The hooks need fur or cloth to cling to, so the seeds stay where they fall.

printables.title: 7 stages on a strip: draw one strip for each player

rules: You need the 21 cards, one stage strip for each player, and one rajma or button for each player.
Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile with the fronts up.
One player is the reader. The reader takes the top card and reads the front aloud, keeping the back hidden.
Every other player puts a rajma on the stage of their strip that failed. Players cover their strips with a hand until all are ready.
The reader reads the back. A player with the rajma on the right stage scores 1 point.
A player who also gives the reason in their own words scores 1 more point. The reader decides, using the back of the card.
The player on the reader's left becomes the next reader.
Playing alone? Read the front, put your rajma on a stage and say your reason aloud. Then turn the card over. Score 1 point for each right stage.
The game ends when the pile is finished. The player with the most points wins. If you play alone, your score out of 21 is your result.

flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Take a rajma seed. Draw seven boxes in a row. Write the seven stages in order.
flow.parent: The seven stages are germination, growth, flowering, pollination, fertilisation, fruit and seed formation, and seed dispersal.
flow.context: This is the first step of Where Did the Cycle Stop. You make the cards and the stage strips.

flow.do: Play the first 10 cards. Read each card aloud. After card 5, ask the question below.
flow.say: Listen to the card. How far did this plant get? Which stage came next and failed? Put your rajma on that box.
flow.kid: Listen to the card. Put your rajma on the stage that failed.

ask.q: How do you tell a pollination card from a fertilisation card?
good: If the pollen never reached the flower, pollination failed.
If the pollen arrived and then something went wrong inside the flower, fertilisation failed.

flow.parent: The hardest pair is pollination and fertilisation. Pollination is the journey of the pollen to the flower. Fertilisation is the joining of the cells afterwards.
flow.context: In this step of Where Did the Cycle Stop you play the first ten cards.

flow.do: Play the last 11 cards and add up the points. Then each player names the stage they think fails most often in real life, and says why.
flow.say: Let's finish the pile. Then tell me which stage you think is the most dangerous for a plant, and why.
flow.kid: Play the rest of the cards. Add up your points.

check.q: Bees carry pollen to a flower, but no seed forms. Which stage most likely failed?
check.why: The pollen reached the flower, so pollination happened. A seed starts only when a male cell joins an egg cell, which is fertilisation. Choosing pollination usually means the two words are still mixed up.

flow.context: This is the last step of Where Did the Cycle Stop. You finish the cards and think about which stage is the riskiest.
