flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Shuffle them. Turn the first card over. Read the lifespan.
flow.context: This is the first step of Longer or Shorter. You make the cards and learn the rules.

flow.do: Play through the pile once. After the game, ask the question below.
flow.say: Read the plant on the card. Will this plant live longer or shorter than the plant before?
flow.kid: Read the plant. Say longer or shorter. Turn the card. Were you right?

ask.q: Which lifespan surprised you most? Why?
good: The banana stem, because the plant looks like a tree but one stem lives only a year.
The bristlecone pine, because the tree is small but is the oldest.
Neelakurinji, because the shrub waits 12 years and flowers once.

flow.parent: Children often guess that the biggest plant is the oldest. The bristlecone pine and the banana stem both break that rule.
flow.context: In this step of Longer or Shorter you play through the 18 lifespan cards.

flow.do: Lay all 18 cards in a row from the shortest life to the longest. Ask your child to find where the annuals end and where the perennials begin.
flow.say: Put all the cards in order, from the shortest life to the longest. Where do the annuals end, and where do the perennials begin?
flow.kid: Put the cards in order, shortest life first. Find where the annuals end.

check.q: Which of these plants has the shortest lifespan?
check.why: A paddy plant is an annual and lives about 5 months. A carrot is a biennial and lives 2 years. A coconut palm is a perennial and lives about 80 years.

flow.context: This is the last step of Longer or Shorter. You put all 18 plants in order of lifespan.

experiments.title: The Bad Year Test: does an annual or a perennial leave more seeds?
experiments.context: In this experiment a die decides the weather for 12 years. You count the seeds that an annual plant and a perennial plant leave in two places: an old grove that is rarely cleared, and a riverbank that is often cleared.
experiments.question: Which plant leaves more seeds in 12 years: an annual or a perennial? Is the answer the same in a place that is rarely cleared and a place that is often cleared?
experiments.predict: Guess before you start. In the old grove, the ground is cleared in about 1 year out of 6. On the riverbank, the ground is cleared in about 3 years out of 6. Which plant will leave more seeds in each place? Why do you think so? Write your two guesses and your reasons.
experiments.fair_test: Both plants face the same years, because one die roll decides the year for both. Each run lasts 12 years. Only one variable is changed between the two places: how often the ground is cleared. Luck decides each roll, so one run is not enough. You do three runs in each place and find the average.

materials.item: die from a ludo or snakes and ladders set (or six paper chits numbered 1 to 6 in a cup)
rajma or button, to stand for the perennial plant
sheet of paper with three boxes drawn in a row: New seedling, One year old, Two years old or more
notebook and pencil for the results table

experiments.record: Fill in one row of the table for each run: three runs for the old grove and three for the riverbank. Then find the average for each plant in each place: add the three totals and divide by 3. Draw a bar chart with four bars, or build four rows of buttons and take a photo.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: average seeds left in 12 years, over three runs
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your own numbers will differ, because your die will fall differently.

setup.art: A die, a rajma seed and a sheet of paper with three boxes in a row labelled New seedling, One year old, and Two years old or more.
setup.caption: 1. Draw three boxes for the perennial. Put the rajma on New seedling.

setup.art: A hand rolling a die beside a notebook row of twelve small boxes, the first few filled with numbers and one number circled.
setup.caption: 2. Roll the die once for each year. Circle the years in which the ground is cleared.

setup.art: The rajma being moved from the box One year old to the box Two years old or more, with a tally of 5s beside it for the annual.
setup.caption: 3. In a good year the annual scores 5. The perennial moves forward, or scores 12 from the last box.

setup.art: A hand-drawn bar chart with four bars, two for the old grove and two for the riverbank.
setup.caption: 4. After three runs in each place, find the averages and draw four bars.

flow.do: 1. Read the rules below with your child. 2. Ask which plant will leave more seeds in each place, and why. 3. Write both guesses and reasons.
flow.say: Each roll of the die is one year. In a good year the annual leaves 5 seeds. The perennial must grow through two good years first, and then leaves 12 seeds in every good year. In a cleared year both leave nothing, and the perennial starts again as a seedling. Which plant will leave more seeds in the old grove? Which on the riverbank? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: One roll is one year. The annual makes 5 seeds in a good year. The perennial grows for two years first. Then they make 12 seeds a year. A cleared year sends the perennial back to the start. Guess who wins in each place. Say why.

ask.q: Which plant do you think will leave more seeds on the riverbank, and why?
good: The perennial, because 12 seeds is more than 5.
The annual, because the perennial keeps getting sent back to the start.
I am not sure, because it depends on the rolls.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. A guess with a reason is what you need. Many children expect the perennial to win everywhere, because 12 is more than 5.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Bad Year Test. You learn the rules and guess which plant leaves more seeds in each place.

flow.do: 1. Draw the three boxes on a sheet of paper. 2. Draw the results table with six rows. 3. Play two practice years together, so the rules are clear.
flow.say: The rajma is the perennial. In a good year, look at where the rajma sits. On the last box, the perennial scores 12. On any other box, the rajma moves one box forward and scores nothing. In a cleared year, the rajma goes back to New seedling.
flow.kid: Draw three boxes in a row. Put the rajma on the first box. Draw the table. Try two practice years.
flow.parent: Check the rule with this row of rolls for the old grove: 4, 6, 2, 1. Years 1 and 2 are good, and the rajma moves forward twice. Year 3 is good, and the perennial scores 12. Year 4 shows a 1, so the ground is cleared and the rajma goes back to the start. The annual has scored 5, 5, 5 and 0.
flow.context: In this step of the Bad Year Test you draw the three boxes for the perennial and the results table.

flow.do: 1. Run 1 in the old grove: roll the die 12 times and write each number. The old grove is cleared only when the die shows 1. 2. Work out the seeds for each plant. 3. Do runs 2 and 3 in the same way.
flow.say: We begin in the old grove. The ground is cleared only when the die shows 1. Roll for 12 years and write every number. Then we count each plant's seeds.
flow.kid: Roll the die 12 times. Write each number. A 1 means cleared. Count the seeds for each plant. Do this three times.

ask.q: Why do both plants use the same 12 rolls?
good: So both plants face the same years.
Then the test is fair, and luck cannot favour one plant.

check.q: In the Bad Year Test, why do you do three runs in each place, and not one?
options: Luck can make one run odd
The die wears out after one run
check.why: Each roll is chance, so one run can go unusually well or badly for a plant. Three runs show the pattern more clearly. Scientists repeat tests for the same reason.

flow.context: In this step of the Bad Year Test you run 12 years in the old grove, three times.

flow.do: 1. Now the riverbank: the ground is cleared when the die shows 1, 2 or 3. 2. Do three runs of 12 years, with the rajma starting on New seedling each time. 3. Fill in the table.
flow.say: Now we move to the riverbank. The river floods often. The ground is cleared when the die shows 1, 2 or 3. Everything else stays the same.
flow.kid: Now a 1, 2 or 3 means cleared. Roll 12 times. Count the seeds. Do this three times.

ask.q: What do you notice about the rajma on the riverbank?
good: The rajma keeps going back to the first box.
The perennial hardly ever reaches the last box.

flow.parent: On the riverbank the perennial needs three good years in a row before scoring. With half the years cleared, that is rare.
flow.context: In this step of the Bad Year Test you run 12 years on the riverbank, three times.

flow.do: 1. For each place, add each plant's three totals and divide by 3. 2. Show the four averages as bars. Draw them, or make four rows of rajma or buttons. 3. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why it happened. 4. Then read the note below together.
flow.say: Find the average for each plant in each place. Show the four averages as bars. Now say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.
flow.kid: Add the three totals. Divide by 3. Show the four averages as bars, drawn or built from buttons. Then tell what happened and why.

ask.q: Which plant left more seeds in the old grove, and which on the riverbank?
good: The perennial in the old grove.
The annual on the riverbank.

ask.q: What does a cleared year cost the annual? What does it cost the perennial?
good: The annual loses one year's seeds.
The perennial loses that year and the growing years too, because the plant starts again.

ask.q: Was there a run that did not fit the pattern? What happened in that run?
good: Yes. In one grove run a 1 came up three times, and the annual won.
No, all the runs fitted.

flow.parent: Usually the perennial leaves more seeds in the old grove, and the annual leaves more on the riverbank. Write down what you really found, even if it differs. The reason: a cleared year costs the annual only one season. It costs the perennial the two growing years as well. Where clearing is rare, the perennial's 12 seeds a year soon overtake the annual's 5. Where clearing is common, the perennial seldom gets three good years in a row. In about one grove run out of four, the annual wins by luck. That is why you repeat the test.
flow.think: Farmers plough a paddy field before every crop. Is a ploughed field more like the old grove or the riverbank?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Bad Year Test. You compare the seeds that the annual and the perennial left in the old grove and on the riverbank.

experiments.title: The Leaf Clock: how old is this plant?
experiments.context: In this three-week experiment you measure how fast a potted plant makes new leaves. Then you use that rate to estimate the age of the plant, and check your estimate against what your family remembers.
experiments.question: Can you work out the age of a plant from how fast the plant makes new leaves? How close does the estimate come to the age your family remembers?
experiments.predict: Guess before you start. How old is this plant? How many new leaf joints will each stem tip make in three weeks? Why do you think so? Write your guesses and your reasons.
experiments.fair_test: You count on three stem tips and not one, because one stem may be unusually fast or slow. The plant stays in the same place and gets the same water for all three weeks. You count a leaf only when the leaf has opened flat. A grown-up writes the plant's remembered age on a folded paper on day 1, so your estimate is made without knowing the answer.

materials.item: potted plant with clear stems, such as a money plant, tulsi, hibiscus or curry leaf plant
pieces of thread, each about 15 centimetres long, in a bright colour
notebook and pencil
folded slip of paper for the grown-up's note

experiments.safety: Tie the threads loosely, so they do not cut into the stem. Take them off at the end.

schedule.what: Guess the plant's age. Tie a thread below the youngest open leaf on three stem tips. A grown-up writes the remembered age on a folded paper.
Count the new leaf joints above each thread.
Make the final count, work out the rate, count all the leaf joints on the longest stem and estimate the age. Open the folded paper.

experiments.record: Fill in the table on days 8, 15 and 22. On day 22, write the rate as leaf joints for one tip in three weeks. Then write your estimate of the plant's age, and the age on the folded paper.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: new leaf joints above the thread on a money plant
example_chart.show: Three stem tips of a money plant, each with a thread tied below the youngest leaf on day 1.
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up. In this example each tip made 2 leaf joints in 3 weeks.

setup.art: A money plant in a pot with a bright thread tied loosely round the stem just below the youngest open leaf at the tip.
setup.caption: 1. Tie a thread below the youngest open leaf on three stem tips.

setup.art: The same stem tip three weeks later, with two new leaves above the thread and a child counting them.
setup.caption: 2. After 8, 15 and 22 days, count the new leaf joints above each thread.

setup.art: A child running a finger along a long vine from the soil to the thread, counting each place where a leaf joins or once joined the stem.
setup.caption: 3. On day 22, count every leaf joint on the longest stem, from the soil to the thread.

setup.art: A notebook with a sum and an estimate in weeks, beside an unfolded slip of paper with a date on it.
setup.caption: 4. Work out your estimate. Then open the folded paper and compare.

flow.do: 1. Choose a potted plant. 2. Ask your child to guess the plant's age and give a reason. 3. Find three stem tips. On each, tie a thread loosely below the youngest leaf that has opened flat. 4. Write the plant's remembered age on a slip of paper, fold it and put it away.
flow.say: A leaf joint is the place where a leaf joins the stem. A plant adds new leaf joints only at the tip of a stem. How old do you think this plant is? How many new leaf joints will each tip make in three weeks? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess how old the plant is. Then tie a thread below the youngest open leaf. Do this on three tips.

ask.q: What makes you think the plant is that old?
good: The plant is big, so they must be old.
The stem is long and has many leaves.
I remember when we bought the plant.

flow.parent: If nobody remembers when the plant arrived, write your best guess and mark it as a guess. A plant with one stem works too. Then use one thread, and say that the result is less sure. If you have no potted plant, sow three rajma in a cup today and use them. Their age will be known exactly.
flow.wait: Leave the plant in the usual place for one week
flow.context: This is the first step of the Leaf Clock. You guess the age of a potted plant and mark three stem tips with thread.

flow.do: Day 8. Count the leaf joints above each thread that carry an open leaf. Write the three numbers.
flow.say: Count only the leaves above the thread that have opened flat. A rolled-up leaf does not count yet.
flow.kid: Count the new open leaves above each thread. Write the three numbers.
flow.context: In this step of the Leaf Clock you make the first count of new leaf joints above the threads.

flow.do: Day 15. Count again and write the three numbers. Ask whether the three tips are growing at the same rate.
flow.say: Count again. Are all three tips making leaves at the same rate? Why might one be slower?
flow.kid: Count again. Write the numbers. Compare the three tips.

ask.q: Why might one stem tip make leaves more slowly than another?
good: That stem gets less light.
That stem is older or thinner.
It may just be chance.

flow.wait: Make the final count one week later
flow.context: In this step of the Leaf Clock you count the new leaf joints for the second time.

flow.do: Day 22. 1. Make the final count. Add the three numbers and divide by 3. This is the rate for one tip in three weeks. 2. On the longest stem, count every leaf joint from the soil to the thread. Count bare joints too. 3. Divide the joints by the rate, and multiply by 3 to get weeks. 4. Open the folded paper and compare. 5. Ask your child to say what they thought, what they found and why the two ages differ.
flow.say: First find the rate: how many leaf joints does one tip make in three weeks? Now count all the joints on the longest stem. How many lots of three weeks did the stem need? Now say what you thought the age was, what you found, and why the two ages may differ.
flow.kid: Find how many leaves one tip makes in three weeks. Count all the leaf joints on the longest stem. Work out the weeks. Open the paper. How close were you?

ask.q: Your estimate and the remembered age are probably different. What could make the estimate too low or too high?
good: The plant grows faster in the rains and slower in the cold months.
Someone may have cut the stem back.
The plant was already some months old when we bought them.
Three weeks is a short time to measure a rate.

ask.q: How would you make the estimate better?
good: Measure the rate for longer, in more than one season.
Count on more stems.
Give the answer as a range.

flow.parent: Example: three tips made 6 leaf joints in three weeks, so one tip makes 2. The longest stem has 40 joints. 40 divided by 2 is 20 lots of three weeks, which is 60 weeks, or about 14 months. An estimate within double or half of the remembered age is a good result. Plants grow faster in warm, wet months, so a rate measured in one season does not fit the whole year. If no new leaves opened in three weeks, the plant is resting. Write that down, and measure again in a warmer month. Scientists estimate the ages of palms and of trees without rings in this same way, and they give a range.
flow.think: A coconut palm makes about 13 leaves a year, and each fallen leaf leaves a scar on the trunk. How could you find the age of a palm?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Leaf Clock. You use the rate of new leaves to estimate the plant's age, and compare the estimate with what your family remembers.

activities.title: Stage Lengths: how much of a life passes before the first flower?
activities.context: In this activity you read a table of how long six plants live and how old they are at their first flower. You turn each pair of numbers into a share of the plant's life, and draw six bars of the same length.

materials.item: pencil, ruler and squared notebook paper
a calculator, or paper for dividing

activities.record: Write each plant's share as a fraction and as a percent. Then draw the six bars, each 10 centimetres long, with a mark where the first flower opens. Or make six paper strips and take a photo.

example_chart.title: Typical lifespans and first flowering ages (rounded)
example_chart.show: Six plants, with the length of the whole life and the age at the first flower.
example_chart.note: The numbers are typical values, rounded. Real plants vary with weather, soil and variety.

setup.art: A table with six plants in rows and two columns of numbers, a pencil pointing at the mustard row.
setup.caption: 1. Read the table. Guess which plant waits longest, as a share of life, before flowering.

setup.art: A division sum 40 ÷ 120 written beside a bar, with the answer one third.
setup.caption: 2. Divide the flowering age by the whole life.

setup.art: Six bars of equal length on squared paper, each with a small flower drawn at a different point along the bar.
setup.caption: 3. Draw six bars of the same length. Mark the first flower on each.

flow.do: 1. Read the table together. 2. Ask which plant spends the biggest share of their life growing before the first flower. 3. Write the guess and the reason.
flow.say: Look at the table. Which plant spends the biggest share of their life growing before the first flower? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Read the table. Look at each plant's whole life and the age at their first flower.

ask.q: Which plant do you think waits longest before flowering? Why?
good: The coconut palm, because 8 years is the longest time.
Paddy, because 90 days is most of 150 days.
I am not sure. I need to divide to compare them.

flow.parent: Many children pick the coconut palm, because 8 years is the biggest number. A share compares a plant with their own life, and not with other plants.
flow.context: This is the first step of Stage Lengths. You read a table of lifespans and guess which plant waits longest before flowering.

flow.do: 1. For each plant, divide the age at first flower by the whole life. Both numbers must be in the same unit. 2. Write the answer as a fraction and as a percent. Example: mustard is 40 ÷ 120 = 1 third, about 33 percent.
flow.say: A share tells us how much of a life passes before the first flower. For mustard, 40 days out of 120 is one third. Now work out the share for the other five plants.
flow.kid: Divide the first flower age by the whole life. Write a fraction and a percent. Do all six plants.
flow.parent: Answers: moong 36 ÷ 90 = 2 fifths, 40 percent. Mustard 1 third, about 33 percent. Paddy 90 ÷ 150 = 3 fifths, 60 percent. Coconut palm 8 ÷ 80 = 1 tenth, 10 percent. Mango 5 ÷ 100 = 1 twentieth, 5 percent. Neelakurinji 12 ÷ 12 = all of the life, 100 percent.
flow.context: In this step of Stage Lengths you work out what share of each plant's life passes before the first flower.

flow.do: 1. Make six bars, each 10 centimetres long. Draw them, or cut six paper strips. 2. Mark the share on each bar with a small flower or a dot. 3. Ask your child to say what they thought, what they found, and why. 4. Ask the question below.
flow.say: Show each plant's whole life as a bar 10 centimetres long. Put a flower at the place where the first flower opens. Say what you thought, what you found, and why you think the pattern is there.
flow.kid: Make six bars, each 10 centimetres long, drawn or cut from paper. Mark the first flower on each. Then compare the bars.

ask.q: What pattern do you see between the annuals and the trees?
good: The annuals flower after a third or more of their life.
The trees flower after a small share of their life, so most of their life is spent flowering.
Neelakurinji is the odd one, because the shrub flowers only at the very end.

flow.parent: Moong, mustard and paddy flower after 33 to 60 percent of their life. Coconut and mango flower after 5 to 10 percent, so most of their long lives are spent making flowers and fruit. This fits the trade-off: a tree spends years building roots and wood first, and then has many seasons to use them.

check.q: A tree lives 100 years and first flowers at 5 years. What share of the life passes before the first flower?
check.why: 5 ÷ 100 = 1 twentieth, which is 5 percent. Choosing one fifth usually means dividing 100 by 5 and reading the answer the wrong way round.

flow.context: This is the last step of Stage Lengths. You draw the six bars and look for a pattern between short lives and long lives.

activities.title: Kitchen Plant Sort: annual, biennial or perennial?
activities.context: In this activity you write the names of 14 plants from a kitchen on slips of paper. You sort them into annuals, biennials and perennials, and then find which ones are farmed in a different way from how they live naturally.

materials.item: 14 paper slips, one for each plant name
pencil
a kitchen shelf, to check what your family really cooks with

activities.record: Write three lists: annuals, biennials and perennials. Put a star by each plant that farmers grow in a different way from how the plant lives on their own.

setup.art: Fourteen paper slips with plant names in a heap beside three labelled columns on a table.
setup.caption: 1. Write 14 plant names on slips. Make three columns.

setup.art: A hand placing the slip 'carrot' in the column labelled Biennial.
setup.caption: 2. Sort each slip into one column.

setup.art: Three slips with stars on them: ginger, sugarcane and onion.
setup.caption: 3. Put a star on the plants that farmers grow in a different way.

flow.do: 1. Write these names on slips: rice, wheat, moong, groundnut, carrot, cabbage, onion, coconut, tamarind, curry leaf, pepper, banana, ginger and sugarcane. 2. Ask your child to guess the group for each, and to say why.
flow.say: Here are 14 plants from a kitchen. Sort them into annual, biennial and perennial. For each one, say why you put them there.
flow.kid: Write 14 plant names on slips. Guess the group for each. Say why.
flow.parent: An annual lives one season. A biennial flowers in the second year. A perennial lives more than two years. Do not correct yet. Listen to the reasons.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Kitchen Plant Sort. You write 14 plant names and make a first guess at their groups.

flow.do: 1. Check the sort with this key. Annuals: rice, wheat, moong, groundnut. Biennials: carrot, cabbage, onion. Perennials: coconut, tamarind, curry leaf, pepper, banana, ginger, sugarcane. 2. Ask which plants surprised your child.
flow.say: Here is the true sort. Which plants surprised you? Banana looks like a tree but has no wood. Sugarcane and ginger look like crops that die each year, but both are perennials.
flow.kid: Check your sort with the key. Move any slip that was in the wrong group.

ask.q: Which plant surprised you, and what did you expect?
good: Banana, because I thought a plant with no wood must live a short time.
Ginger, because we buy it fresh each time.
Onion, because I did not know it flowers in the second year.

flow.parent: A banana clump lives for years, because new stems grow from the base. Each stem fruits once and dies. A woody stem is a clue for a perennial but not a sure test.
flow.context: In this step of the Kitchen Plant Sort you check your groups against the true groups.

flow.do: 1. Put a star on each plant that farmers grow in a different way from how the plant lives on their own. 2. Check: carrot, cabbage and onion are harvested in the first year, before they flower. Ginger and sugarcane are dug up or cut after a year or so. 3. Ask the question below.
flow.say: Farmers often grow a plant differently from how the plant lives on their own. Carrot and onion are biennials, but we eat them in the first year.
flow.kid: Put a star by each plant that farmers harvest early.

ask.q: Why do farmers harvest a carrot in the first year?
good: The root is full of stored food in year one, which is what we eat.
In year two the carrot spends the food on flowers and the root becomes tough and woody.

flow.parent: A biennial stores food in its root in year one. In year two the plant uses that food to flower. A farmer who wants seed from carrots must leave some plants for a second year.

check.q: A carrot plant is left in the ground for a second year. What happens to the stored food in the root?
options: The plant uses the food to flower and make seed
The root grows twice as big
The root turns into a leaf
check.why: A biennial stores food in year one and spends it on flowers and seeds in year two. A bigger root is a common guess, but the root shrinks as the food is used.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Kitchen Plant Sort. You find which plants are farmed in a different way from how they live.

activities.title: Who Senses the Night? Read the plant experiments
activities.context: In this activity you read the results of five simple experiments on chrysanthemum plants, which flower when nights grow long. You decide which part of the plant senses the night, and what must pass from that part to the buds.

materials.item: pencil and paper
coloured pencils

activities.record: Draw a plant with leaves and a bud. Draw an arrow for the signal and write what you think the signal does. Or tell it out loud to your grown-up.

example_chart.title: Simplified results from experiments on chrysanthemum plants
example_chart.show: Five tests in which leaves and buds get different night lengths, with the result of each.
example_chart.note: These results are simplified from experiments done by scientists such as Knott in 1934 and Chailakhyan in 1936. Chrysanthemums flower when nights are long.

setup.art: A chrysanthemum plant with one leaf under a small paper cap and the bud above left uncovered.
setup.caption: 1. In some tests, only the leaves or only the buds get the night.

setup.art: A table of five tests with the word Yes or No at the end of each row.
setup.caption: 2. Read the five results.

setup.art: A plant drawing with an arrow running up the stem from a leaf to a bud.
setup.caption: 3. Draw what must travel from the leaf to the bud.

flow.do: 1. Read the table with your child. 2. Explain that a chrysanthemum flowers when nights are long. 3. Ask which part they think senses the night: the leaves or the buds. Ask for a reason.
flow.say: Chrysanthemums flower when the nights grow long. In these tests, the leaves and the buds sometimes get different nights. Which part do you think senses the night, the leaves or the buds? Why?
flow.kid: Read the five tests. Look at which parts get the long night.

ask.q: Which part do you think senses the night, and why?
good: The buds, because the buds are the part that opens as a flower.
The leaves, because the leaves are the part that faces the sky.

flow.parent: Either guess is fair before the table is read closely. Look for the reason the child gives.
flow.context: This is the first step of Who Senses the Night. You read five test results and make a first guess.

flow.do: 1. Compare tests 3 and 4. 2. Ask what changed between them. 3. Ask what test 5 shows. 4. Ask for the claim, the evidence and the reasoning.
flow.say: Look at tests 3 and 4. In test 3 the buds get long nights and the plant does not flower. In test 4 only the leaves get long nights and the plant flowers. What does that show? What does test 5 add?
flow.kid: Compare tests 3 and 4. Point to what is different between them.

ask.q: Which part senses the night, and what is your evidence?
good: The leaves. In test 4 only the leaves got long nights, and the plant flowered.
In test 3 the buds got long nights, but the plant did not flower.

ask.q: What does test 5 show?
good: Without leaves, the plant does not flower, even if the buds get long nights.
The leaves are needed.

flow.parent: The leaves sense the night. The buds make the flowers. So something must pass from the leaves to the buds, because the buds open without sensing the night themselves.
flow.context: In this step of Who Senses the Night you compare the tests to find which part senses the night.

flow.do: 1. Draw a plant with leaves and a bud. Or tell your grown-up where the signal travels, using your finger. 2. Draw an arrow from a leaf to the bud and label it 'signal'. 3. Ask your child to predict a new test: a leaf from a flowering plant is joined to a plant on short nights. Will that plant flower? Then read the note.
flow.say: Something must travel from the leaves to the buds. Scientists named it florigen. Here is a new test. A leaf from a flowering plant is joined to a plant that has short nights. What do you think happens, and why?
flow.kid: Draw the plant and the signal arrow. Or trace it with your finger. Then guess what happens in the new test.

ask.q: In the new test, will the plant on short nights flower? Why?
good: Yes, because the joined leaf sends the signal that makes buds flower.
No, because that plant never got long nights.

flow.parent: Real grafts like this made plants flower, which is the evidence that a signal exists. The signal is a small protein, found in 2007, and it is carried in the plant's sap. Not all plants work in the same way. This test describes plants that need long nights, such as chrysanthemum.

check.q: Only the leaves of a chrysanthemum plant get long nights. The buds get short nights. What does the plant do?
options: Flowers, because the leaves sense the night and send a signal
Does not flower, because the buds are in short nights
check.why: The leaves sense the length of the night and send a signal to the buds, as in test 4. Choosing the second answer usually means thinking that the part that opens must be the part that senses.

flow.context: This is the last step of Who Senses the Night. You draw the signal and predict a new test.

activities.title: Perennial Rice or Annual Rice? A three-sided debate
activities.context: In this activity three people take the sides in a real argument among scientists: should our grain crops live for many years? Each person gives one reason, then each answers the others.

materials.item: paper and pencil
a timer or a phone clock

activities.record: Each person writes one point for their side and one fair point from another side. Then each writes their final view.

setup.art: Three people sitting round a table, each with a card showing a role: breeder, crop scientist, farmer.
setup.caption: 1. Each person takes one of three roles.

setup.art: One person speaking for one minute while another holds a phone timer.
setup.caption: 2. Each role speaks for one minute.

setup.art: Three pieces of paper, each with one point written for a side and one point from another side.
setup.caption: 3. Write one fair point for another side.

flow.do: 1. Choose three roles. The breeder of perennial rice says: sow once, harvest for years, roots hold the soil, and breeding can raise yields. The crop scientist says: a plant that saves food for next year has less for grain, and weeds and disease build up. The farmer says: grow both, with trees and perennials for the soil, and annual grain between. 2. Each person reads their role card.
flow.say: Three people take part in this debate. One breeds perennial rice. One works on annual grain. One farms both kinds. Choose a role. Think for one minute about your best reason.
flow.kid: Choose a role. Think about your best reason for one minute.
flow.parent: Perennial rice PR23 was bred in Yunnan, China, and gave yields close to annual rice in tests. Kernza, a perennial grass grain grown in Kansas, still gives much less grain than wheat. The facts are real, and the argument about the future is open.
flow.context: This is the first step of the debate about perennial rice. You choose a role and prepare one reason.

flow.do: 1. Each role speaks for one minute. 2. Each person then says one fair point that another role made.
flow.say: Each role speaks for one minute. Then say one point from another role that you think is fair.
flow.kid: Speak for one minute. Then say one fair point from another role.

ask.q: Which fair point from another side was the hardest to say?
good: That perennial grains give less grain so far.
That deep roots hold soil in heavy rain.
That both crops can share one farm.

flow.parent: Do not pick a winner. A good debate ends with each person naming something fair from another side.
flow.context: In this step of the debate about perennial rice, each role speaks and then names a fair point from another side.

flow.do: 1. Each person says or writes their final view in two sentences. 2. Ask the question below.
flow.say: Say or write your own view in two sentences. Think about what could make you change it.
flow.kid: Say or write your own view in two sentences.

ask.q: What evidence would change your mind?
good: A perennial rice that yields as much as annual rice in many places.
A test showing weeds or disease building up in unploughed fields.

flow.parent: The best answers name evidence that could be gathered, such as yields over ten years.

check.q: Which fact is the strongest reason for growing a perennial grain?
options: Roots stay in the soil all year and hold it in heavy rain
Perennial grains always give more grain
check.why: Roots in the ground all year hold soil. The other two are not true: perennial grains so far give less grain than annual grains, and size does not set the yield.

flow.context: This is the last step of the debate about perennial rice. You write your own view and say what evidence would change it.

projects.title: Same Seed, Different Start Day: does methi flower at the same age or on the same date?
projects.context: In this 12-week project you sow methi (fenugreek) in two pots, three weeks apart, and record the day each stage begins. You find out whether the two plants flower at the same age, or on the same date.
projects.question: Does a methi plant flower after the same number of days from sowing, or on the same date, whatever day the seeds were sown?
projects.predict: Pot A is sown on day 1 and pot B on day 22. If both flower at the same age, pot B will flower 21 days after pot A. If both flower on the same date, they will flower together. Which will happen? Why do you think so?

materials.item: whole methi seeds (fenugreek) from the kitchen, about 24
pots or tubs about 20 centimetres wide and 15 centimetres deep, with holes at the bottom
soil from a nursery or garden, about 2 kilograms for each pot
two labels, A and B
a ruler
a mug for watering
notebook and pencil

projects.safety: Wash hands after handling soil. Methi seeds are safe to eat, but do not let a young child put soil or seeds in their mouth.

schedule.what: Predict. Sow 12 seeds in pot A, 1 centimetre deep and 4 centimetres apart. Water gently. Put the pot by a bright window.
Count the seedlings in pot A. Thin to the 6 strongest by snipping the others at soil level.
Sow 12 seeds in pot B in the same way, in the same window. Keep watering pot A as before.
Thin pot B to 6 seedlings. Write the date each seedling count was made.
Look at both pots. Write the age of each pot in days, and the leaves you can count.
Look for the first flower buds in pot A. Write the day and the date.
Look for first flowers in pot A and pot B. Write the day and the date for each.
Look for the first thin pods. Write the day and the date.
Compare the two pots and write a conclusion.

projects.record: Make a table with the rows: seedlings up, first flower bud, first open flower, first pod. For each row write the calendar date and the plant's age in days, for pot A and for pot B. Then write a claim, the evidence and the reasoning.
projects.fair_test: Both pots have the same soil, pot size, number of seeds, window and watering. Only the sowing day changes. Never pick leaves for eating from either pot, because picking changes the growth. Water each pot with one mug when the top centimetre of soil is dry.

setup.art: Two pots labelled A and B on a windowsill, pot A with tall seedlings and pot B with just-sown soil.
setup.caption: 1. Sow pot A on day 1. Sow pot B three weeks later.

setup.art: A notebook table with rows for seedlings, bud, flower and pod, and columns for date and age in days for each pot.
setup.caption: 2. Write the date and the age at each stage.

setup.art: A methi plant with small white flowers and a long thin pod beside a ruler.
setup.caption: 3. Look for the first flower and the first pod.

flow.do: 1. Fill two pots with soil and label them A and B. 2. Sow 12 seeds in pot A, 1 centimetre deep, 4 centimetres apart. Water gently. 3. Ask your child to predict when pot B will flower, and to say why. 4. Write the prediction in the notebook.
flow.say: Pot A is sown today. Pot B will be sown in three weeks. Will pot B flower after the same number of days as pot A, or on the same date as pot A? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Sow 12 seeds in pot A, 1 centimetre deep. Water it gently.

ask.q: Will pot B flower at the same age as pot A, or on the same date? Why?
good: The same age, because each plant counts their own days.
The same date, because the season tells them when to flower.
Somewhere in between, because both age and season matter.

flow.parent: Sow between October and February in most of India. In the rains seeds may rot, and in the hottest months the plants bolt early. Methi seeds germinate in 3 to 5 days in a warm room. Both answers are fair at this stage.
flow.wait: Check the pot every day for 4 days
flow.context: This is the first step of the Same Seed, Different Start Day project. You sow pot A and make a prediction.

flow.do: 1. On day 5, count the seedlings in pot A. 2. Snip the weaker ones at soil level, so 6 remain. 3. Write the date.
flow.say: Count the seedlings. Keep the 6 strongest, and snip the others at soil level, so that each plant has room. Write today's date.
flow.kid: Count the seedlings. Keep 6. Snip the others at soil level.
flow.parent: If fewer than 6 seedlings came up, keep them all. Do not pull seedlings up by the roots, because that disturbs the others.
flow.context: In this step of the Same Seed, Different Start Day project you thin pot A to six seedlings.

flow.do: 1. On day 22, sow pot B in the same way and in the same window. 2. Write pot A's age on that day. 3. Look at pot A. How many leaves has a plant made?
flow.say: Now sow pot B in the same way, in the same window. Pot A is 21 days old.
flow.kid: Sow pot B in the same way as pot A. Then look closely at both pots.

ask.q: Which stage is pot A in now, and which is pot B in?
good: Pot A has leaves, and pot B is just sown.
Pot A is growing, and pot B is germinating.

flow.parent: Pot A should be a small leafy plant by now. Both pots must stand in the same window.
flow.wait: Look at both pots each week
flow.context: In this step of the Same Seed, Different Start Day project you sow pot B, three weeks after pot A.

flow.do: 1. Look at both pots on days 36, 50 and 64. 2. Each time, write down the stage each pot has reached, with the date and the age in days. 3. Check the soil. Water with one mug if the top centimetre is dry.
flow.say: Look at both pots. Write the stage each has reached, today's date, and the age of each pot in days. Which pot is further along?
flow.kid: Look at both pots. Take a photo of each. Write the stage of each pot, the date and the age in days.

ask.q: Is pot B catching up with pot A? What do you think is making that happen?
good: Pot B is younger, so maybe the weather is telling both pots when to flower.
Pot B is growing at the same speed as pot A did at that age.

flow.parent: Methi first flowers about 6 to 9 weeks after sowing, with small white flowers. Warm weather makes plants flower sooner. If pot B is warmer than pot A was at that age, pot B may flower at a younger age. That is a real result worth writing down.
flow.context: In this step of the Same Seed, Different Start Day project you record the stages of both pots on three days.

flow.do: 1. On day 78 write the date and age of the first pod in each pot. 2. On day 85, fill in the table. 3. Compare the ages in days and the dates, for pot A and pot B. 4. Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw, and why it happened.
flow.say: Fill in the table. Compare the age at each stage for pot A and pot B. Compare the dates too. Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.
flow.kid: Fill in the table. Compare ages and dates. Say what you thought, what you saw, and why.

ask.q: Did pot B flower at the same age as pot A, or on the same date, or in between?
good: In between: pot B flowered at a younger age, but later than pot A.
At the same age.
On nearly the same date.

ask.q: What could have made the result different from your prediction?
good: The weather got warmer, so pot B flowered younger.
The days got longer or shorter.
One pot had more light.

flow.parent: There are three possible results. If pot B flowered about 21 days later, the plants count their own age. If pot B flowered on the same date, the season decides. A result in between is the most common, because a plant needs both enough size and a suitable season, as the florigen story showed. Whatever happens, write what really happened. If a pot did not flower by day 85, write that down and note the temperature and light.
flow.think: Why might a farmer sow methi on three different dates instead of one?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Same Seed, Different Start Day project. You compare the two pots and decide if methi flowers by age or by date.

challenges.title: Fit the Plant to the Field: two fields, two plants
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. A family has two fields. The low field is cleared by floods when the die shows 1, 2 or 3. The high field is cleared only when the die shows 1. You choose which plant to put in each field, then test the plan with the rules of the Bad Year Test.
challenges.problem: Choose an annual or a perennial for the low field, and an annual or a perennial for the high field. Then test the plan over 12 years and add up the seeds from both fields.
constraints: Use the same rules as the Bad Year Test. The annual gives 5 seeds in a good year. The perennial gives 12 seeds in a good year after two good years of growing.
Roll one die for the low field and one die for the high field each year. Use a different colour of rajma or button for each field.
Do three runs of 12 years and find the average total.
materials: two dice, or one die rolled twice
two rajma or buttons of different colours
the three-box strip from the Bad Year Test
general: Put the annual in the low field and the perennial in the high field.
Put the annual in both fields, because the annual is steady.
Put the perennial in both fields, because 12 seeds is more than 5.
creative: Leave part of the high field as perennial and part as annual, and compare the average.
Choose a different plan for each field after a bad run.
Add a third field where the die clears the ground on 1 or 2, and decide which plant fits best.
challenges.your_turn: Choose your own plan and write your prediction. Test it for three runs. Did the plan do better than putting the same plant in both fields? By how many seeds?

setup.art: Two small drawn fields on paper, the low one marked with a wavy river line and the high one marked with a tree.
setup.caption: 1. Label the low field and the high field.

setup.art: Two dice in front of the fields, one for each field, with a rajma on each three-box strip.
setup.caption: 2. Roll one die for each field every year.

setup.art: A notebook table of three runs with totals for each field and a final sum.
setup.caption: 3. Add the seeds from both fields.

flow.do: 1. Write 'low field' on one paper slip and 'high field' on another. 2. Ask your child to choose a plant for each field and to say why. 3. Write the plan.
flow.say: The low field floods often. The high field is rarely cleared. Which plant will you put in each field? Why?
flow.kid: Put the low field slip and the high field slip side by side. Pick a plant for each.
flow.parent: In the Bad Year Test the annual left more seeds where clearing is common and the perennial where it is rare. Many children now choose the annual for the low field and the perennial for the high field.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Fit the Plant to the Field challenge. You choose a plant for each field.

flow.do: 1. Roll the die for the low field and the die for the high field, 12 times. 2. Count the seeds for each field by the Bad Year Test rules. 3. Add the two totals. 4. Do three runs and find the average.
flow.say: Each year, roll one die for each field. A 1, 2 or 3 clears the low field. Only a 1 clears the high field. Count the seeds for each field, and add them.
flow.kid: Roll twice each year, once for each field. Count the seeds. Add the totals. Do three runs.
flow.parent: Example for a low field with an annual: 12 years with 7 cleared years leaves 5 good years, and 5 × 5 = 25 seeds.
flow.context: In this step of the Fit the Plant to the Field challenge you test your plan for three runs of 12 years.

flow.do: 1. Compare the average total of your plan with the average of putting the same plant in both fields. 2. Ask the question below.
flow.say: Compare your total with a plan that puts the same plant in both fields. Did matching the plant to the field help? Say what you thought, what you saw, and why.
flow.kid: Compare your total with the same-plant plan. Say what you thought, what you saw, and why.

ask.q: What would you change in the plan if the low field flooded only on a 1 or a 2?
good: The two plants would give nearly the same seeds, so either could work.
I would test it three times, because the result is too close to call from one run.

flow.parent: With clearing on 1 or 2 (one year in three), the annual averages about 40 seeds and the perennial about 36 in a run. The totals are close, and either plant can win a single run.

check.q: A field is cleared one year in three. In a test, the annual leaves 40 seeds and the perennial 36 on average. What does this tell you?
options: Neither plant is clearly better, so you need more runs
check.why: The averages are close, and one run can go either way. You need more runs before you pick. Choosing the annual because 40 is bigger forgets that chance moves each run.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Fit the Plant to the Field challenge. You compare your plan with a plan that uses one plant everywhere.

challenges.title: The Rare Flowering Calendar: plan your life around plants that flower once in many years
challenges.context: This is a planning challenge. Neelakurinji shrubs flower every 12 years, and the last flowering was in 2018. Muli bamboo in Mizoram flowers about every 48 years, and the last flowering was around 2007. You build a calendar from 2000 to 2100 and find when you can see each one.
challenges.problem: Make a time line from 2000 to 2100 and mark every year in which each plant should flower. Then work out how old you will be in each flowering year.
constraints: Use squared notebook paper with one box for each 2 years, so the time line has 50 boxes.
Use one colour for neelakurinji and another colour for muli bamboo.
Say that the years are expected years, because the real cycles can vary by a year or more.
general: Count on by 12 from 2018 for neelakurinji: 2030, 2042, 2054, and so on.
Count on by 48 from 2007 for the bamboo: 2055 and 2103.
Write your own birth year and subtract it from each flowering year.
creative: Draw a bamboo and a shrub on the time line in their flowering years.
Invent a made-up plant that flowers every 16 years from 2018. Mark it too, and find the year when it flowers with neelakurinji.
Plan a family trip for one of the years.
challenges.your_turn: Choose the flowering you most want to see. Say how old you will be, and what you would look for.

setup.art: A long strip of squared paper marked with years from 2000 to 2100, a blue mark for 2018 and a green mark for 2007.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the time line from 2000 to 2100. One box is 2 years.

setup.art: Blue marks at 2018, 2030, 2042 and 2054 along the strip.
setup.caption: 2. Mark the neelakurinji years in blue.

setup.art: A green mark at 2055 and a child pointing to the gap between 2054 and 2055.
setup.caption: 3. Mark the bamboo years in green.

flow.do: 1. Draw the time line. 2. Mark 2018 in blue and 2007 in green. 3. Ask your child which plant will flower sooner after 2018.
flow.say: Neelakurinji flowered in 2018, and bamboo flowered around 2007. Which will flower first after today? Make a guess, then we will work it out.
flow.kid: Draw the time line. Mark 2018 and 2007. Guess which plant flowers next.
flow.parent: The next neelakurinji flowering is expected in 2030. The bamboo is expected around 2055. Both are expected years only.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Rare Flowering Calendar challenge. You draw a time line and mark the last flowering of each plant.

flow.do: 1. Count on by 12 from 2018 and mark each year in blue until 2100. 2. Count on by 48 from 2007 and mark each year in green. 3. Check the two colours: do the blue years and the green years ever fall in the same year?
flow.say: Count on by 12 from 2018 and mark each flowering. Then count on by 48 from 2007. Do the two plants ever flower in the same year?
flow.kid: Count on by 12 from 2018. Count on by 48 from 2007. Mark the years.
flow.parent: Neelakurinji: 2030, 2042, 2054, 2066, 2078, 2090. Bamboo: 2055 and 2103. The two never fall in the same year before 2100. 2054 and 2055 are one year apart, which is a good chance to talk about how real cycles can vary.
flow.context: In this step of the Rare Flowering Calendar challenge you mark the expected flowering years of both plants.

flow.do: 1. Write your own birth year. 2. Subtract it from each flowering year to find your age. 3. Ask your child to choose the flowering they most want to see.
flow.say: Subtract your birth year from each flowering year. How old will you be? Which flowering do you most want to see, and why?
flow.kid: Work out your age at each flowering. Choose the one you most want to see.

ask.q: How many neelakurinji flowerings will you see before you are 60? How do you know?
good: A child born around 2016 will be 14 in 2030, 26 in 2042, 38 in 2054 and 50 in 2066, so 4 flowerings.
I count the flowering years that fall before my 60th birthday.

flow.parent: A child born in 2016 is 14 in 2030, 26 in 2042, 38 in 2054, 50 in 2066 and 62 in 2078. So that child sees 4 flowerings before turning 60, and will see the bamboo at about age 39.

check.q: A plant flowers every 12 years. It flowered in 2018. In which year will it flower after 2042?
check.why: 2042 + 12 = 2054. Choosing 2052 or 2056 usually means adding 10 or 14 instead of the cycle length.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Rare Flowering Calendar challenge. You work out how old you will be at each flowering.

items.p: Put the seven stages of a flowering plant's life in order.
items.why: The stages always come in this order. The seeds from the last stage start the first stage again. A strong answer says that if one stage fails, no new seeds are made.

items.p: A bee leaves pollen on a flower. What must happen before a seed can start to form?
opts: A male cell joins an egg cell inside the flower
items.why: After pollination, a male cell from the pollen joins an egg cell inside the flower. That is fertilisation, and a seed starts only after that. Choosing the petals falling off mixes up a sign that often follows with the cause.

items.p: Match each stage to what happens in it.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each stage has one job. A strong answer can say why pollination and fertilisation are different stages: one carries the pollen, and the other joins the cells.
pairs: Germination
a seed takes in water, and a root and shoot grow out
Pollination
pollen is carried to the female part of a flower
Fertilisation
a male cell joins an egg cell inside the flower
Fruit and seed formation
fertilised egg cells grow into seeds inside a fruit
Seed dispersal
seeds are carried away from the parent plant

items.p: A plant that goes through the whole life cycle in one growing season and then dies is called an ____.
items.why: Annuals such as paddy, moong and mustard make seeds and die within one season. Their seeds wait for the next season.

items.p: True or false: a fern makes flowers, but no seeds.
items.why: False. A fern makes no flowers and no seeds. A fern makes spores, which are single cells. A strong answer says what ferns make instead.

items.p: Sort these plants into annual, biennial and perennial.
items.a: see items
items.why: Paddy, moong and wheat live one season. Carrot and cabbage flower in their second year. Mango, coconut and tamarind live for many years. A strong answer gives the clue for each group.

items.p: Which stage does a fern never have?
items.why: A fern has no flowers, so a fern has no pollination. A fern spore germinates, the fern grows, and spores are carried away by wind. Choosing seed dispersal forgets that spores are dispersed too.

items.p: A pumpkin plant has many flowers, but no insect ever visits them. Which stage fails? Explain why no fruit grows.
items.a: Pollination fails. Pumpkin pollen must be carried by insects from one flower to another. Without pollination, no male cell can reach an egg cell, so no seed starts and no fruit grows.
items.why: A strong answer names pollination, says what is missing (a carrier for the pollen), and links this to why fertilisation and fruit cannot follow.

items.p: Which plant can live for several thousand years?
items.why: Bristlecone pines in California have been counted at nearly 5,000 years. Mustard, moong and paddy live a few months.

items.p: Three of these are annuals. Which one is the odd one out?
items.why: Paddy, mustard and moong live one season. A mango tree lives for a hundred years or more.

items.p: True or false: a plant with no wood in the stem cannot be a perennial.
items.why: False. Banana and ginger have no wood, but both live for many years. A strong answer names banana or ginger.

items.p: Draw a flower where pollen has landed, and label: pollen grain, pollen tube, egg cell.
a: Pollen grain on the top of the flower's female part
Egg cell at the bottom, inside the flower
items.why: After pollination, the pollen grain grows a thin tube down to an egg cell. A male cell travels down the tube. A strong drawing shows the tube joining the pollen grain to the egg cell.
items.art: A blank outline of a cut-open flower showing the female part from the top to the bottom.

items.p: A mustard plant lives 120 days and first flowers at day 40. What share of the life passes before the first flower?
items.why: 40 ÷ 120 = 1 third. One half would need 60 days, and one quarter would need 30 days.

items.p: Think about the Bad Year Test. On the riverbank, why did the perennial usually leave fewer seeds than the annual?
items.a: On the riverbank, the ground was cleared in about half of the years. Each time, the perennial went back to the start and had to grow for two years again before making 12 seeds. The annual lost only one season, and made 5 seeds in each good year.
items.why: A strong answer uses evidence from the test: how often the rajma went back to the start, and what a cleared year cost each plant.

items.p: True or false: pollination and fertilisation are the same stage.
items.why: False. Pollination is the carrying of pollen to the flower. Fertilisation happens afterwards, inside the flower, when a male cell joins an egg cell.

items.p: Which of these foods comes from a perennial plant?
items.why: Pepper grows on a vine that lives for many years. Rice, wheat and moong are annuals.

items.p: On a riverbank that floods often, why do annuals do well?
opts: A flood costs an annual only one season
Annuals like water more than perennials do
Floods carry away the perennials' seeds
items.why: A flood kills the grown plants. An annual loses only the seeds that season, and the seeds in the soil grow when the water goes down. A perennial loses the years it spent growing.

items.p: A young mango tree makes no mango for about five years. Why would a plant grow so long before making seeds?
items.a: The tree spends food on roots, wood and leaves first. A big tree with deep roots can then make a large crop every year for a hundred years. Food spent on seeds early would leave less for growing.
items.why: A strong answer uses the word trade-off, or says that food spent on seeds cannot be spent on staying alive.

items.p: Where would you expect mostly annuals, and where mostly perennials?
items.a: see items
items.why: Annuals do well where the ground is cleared often, and perennials do well where it is left alone. A strong answer names the disturbance for each place.
items: a river sandbank after a flood
an old forest in the Western Ghats

items.p: Food spent on seeds leaves less for roots and wood. A choice like this is called a ____.
items.why: A trade-off means that having more of one thing means having less of another.

items.p: A coconut palm first flowers at 8 years and lives 80 years. What share of life passes before the first flower?
items.why: 8 ÷ 80 = 1 tenth. One eighth comes from dividing 80 by 10 by mistake.

items.p: After a field is cleared and left alone, plants change in a regular order. Put them in order, first to last.
items.why: Annual weeds arrive first, because they flower young. Perennial grasses and herbs follow, then shrubs, and after many years trees.

items.p: True or false: the biggest tree in a forest is always the oldest.
items.why: False. The oldest trees counted so far are small bristlecone pines on dry mountains. A tree in rich soil can grow large in a few hundred years.

items.p: A chrysanthemum plant flowers when the nights are long. Which part of the plant senses the length of the night?
items.why: Scientists covered or lit different parts of plants. They found that the leaves sense the night and send a signal to the buds.

items.p: Claim: a plant that lives longer is more successful. Do you agree? Use evidence from the Bad Year Test.
items.a: I do not fully agree. In the Bad Year Test, the perennial left more seeds in the old grove, but the annual left more on the riverbank. Which plant leaves more seeds depends on how often the ground is cleared. So a longer life is not always more successful.
items.why: A strong answer uses results from the test, names both places, and says what decides the winner.

items.p: Three of these are disturbances that clear plants from the ground. Which one is the odd one out?
items.why: Floods, landslides and ploughing clear plants from the ground. A slow shower waters the plants and does not clear them.

items.p: Match each plant to the way the plant flowers.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These four plants flower in four different ways. A strong answer can say which of them is an annual (bhindi) and which are perennials.
pairs: Neelakurinji
grows for 12 years, flowers once, then dies
Talipot palm
grows for decades, flowers once, then dies
Coconut palm
flowers all through the year for decades
Bhindi
each flower lasts only one day

items.p: A coconut trunk shows 260 leaf scars. A palm makes about 13 leaves a year. About how old is the palm?
items.why: 260 ÷ 13 = 20 years. Choosing 260 forgets that each year makes about 13 scars.

items.p: Your Leaf Clock estimate was lower than the remembered age. Give two reasons the estimate could be too low.
items.a: The plant may grow faster in the rains than in the three weeks I measured, so my rate was too slow. Someone may have cut the stem, so I counted fewer joints than the plant once had.
items.why: A strong answer gives two different reasons, and links each one to how the rate or the count was measured.

items.p: True or false: rice, wheat and maize together give people about half of their food energy.
items.why: True. All three are annuals, and each puts a large share of the plant into grain.

items.p: A cyclone blew down thousands of coconut palms in Tamil Nadu in 2018. Two farmers talk about what to plant.
items.a: A strong answer sees the trade-off: the annual recovers fast but must be sown every year, and the perennial recovers slowly but then gives for decades. It names one fair point from each side.
items.why: There is no single winner. Each way of living suits a different kind of risk.

views.says: My field is ploughed and sown every year. After a storm I sow again, and I have a crop in one season.
A new palm takes about eight years to bear. But a grown palm gives nuts every month for decades.

items.ask: Which farmer is better prepared for a storm? Which is better prepared for a long future? Give one reason for each.

items.p: Draw a time line from 0 to 100 years. Mark where moong, coconut and mango end.
items.a: Moong ends at about 3 months, so the mark is almost at 0. The coconut palm ends at about 80 years. The mango tree ends at about 100 years.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the moong mark as a tiny dot close to 0, and the two trees far along the line.
items.art: A blank time line from 0 to 100 years with ticks every 10 years.

items.p: Scientists disagree about whether perennial grains can replace rice and wheat.
items.a: A strong answer chooses a side, backs it with a fact such as the trade-off between seeds and roots, and names a fair point from another side.
items.why: This is a real argument. Evidence from fields over many years will help to settle it.

views.says: A perennial grain is sown once and harvested for years. Deep roots hold the soil, and breeding can raise the yield.

views.who: A crop scientist who works on annual grains
views.says: A plant that saves food for next year has less to put into grain. Weeds and disease build up in a field that is never ploughed.

views.who: A farmer who grows both kinds
views.says: Trees and perennial crops can hold the soil, and annual grain can grow between them. One field can hold both.

items.ask: Which side do you agree with? Give one reason. Then give one fair point from another side.

items.p: Scientists disagree about whether very old trees age.
items.a: A strong answer names evidence, such as healthy seeds from old trees or the build-up of rot and damage, and names a test that could settle the question.
items.why: Both views fit what we know today. The question is open.

views.who: A scientist who says some trees do not age
views.says: A tree makes new leaves, buds and wood every year. A pine of 4,700 years made seeds as healthy as those of a young pine.

views.who: A scientist who says trees age slowly
views.says: No tree lives for ever. Damage and rot build up, and old trees grow very little.

items.ask: Which scientist do you agree with? What evidence would help to decide?

items.p: Marigolds may flower sooner when nights are longer. Plan a fair test with pots: what you change, measure and keep the same.
items.a: Change: the hours of dark each night, for example by covering one pot for 14 hours and leaving another uncovered. Measure: the day each pot opens its first flower. Keep the same: the plant kind, the pot, the soil, the water and the temperature. Use three pots in each group, because one pot can differ by chance.
items.why: A strong answer changes one thing, measures the day of the first flower, keeps the rest the same, and repeats the test.

items.p: A tree core has 120 rings, then a rotten hollow that may hide 20 more. Give the age as a range.
items.a: The tree is at least 120 years old. With the rotten centre, it could be about 120 to 140 years old. I give a range, because I cannot count rings that have rotted.
items.why: A strong answer says 'at least 120', gives a range with a reason, and does not claim an exact age.

items.p: When a die clears the ground on a 1 or a 2, what do you expect in the Bad Year Test?
opts: Neither plant wins every run, and the totals are close
items.why: When clearing happens one year in three, the annual averages about 40 seeds and the perennial about 36. Either can win a single run, so you need several runs.

items.p: If the perennial needed five growing years instead of two, what would happen to the seeds? Why?
items.a: It would leave fewer seeds. Each cleared year would send it back to the start, and it would need five good years in a row before making any seeds. In the old grove that would happen less often, and on the riverbank almost never.
items.why: A strong answer says the perennial leaves fewer seeds, and explains it with the longer wait and the cleared years.

items.p: Which statement about the seven stages is true?
opts: All flowering plants follow the same seven stages
Perennials have more stages than annuals
items.why: A mustard plant fits the seven stages into four months, and a banyan spreads them over centuries. The order is the same.

items.p: True or false: a plant that flowers once and then dies, like the talipot palm, must be an annual.
items.why: False. The talipot palm lives for decades, so it is a perennial. It flowers only once, at the end of its life.

items.p: A core from a bristlecone pine shows 4,600 rings. Why do scientists say 'more than 4,600 years'?
opts: Some rings may be missing, so the count is low
The core is always cut in half
items.why: A tree can miss a ring in a very dry year, and the centre may have rotted away. The real age is probably higher than the count.

items.p: Match each way of finding a plant's age to what limits that way.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each method suits some plants and not others. A strong answer says why an honest age is given as a range.
pairs: A record of the planting
works only if someone wrote it down
Counting tree rings
needs yearly rings, which many tropical trees lack
Carbon dating
gives a range, not an exact year
Counting leaf scars
is only as good as the rate of new leaves

items.p: Which of these are evidence, and which are opinion?
items.a: see items
items.why: Evidence is something that was counted or measured, and that others could check. An opinion is a judgement that no count can settle.
items: Perennial rice gave eight harvests in four years
Old trees are wiser than young ones
The banyan is the best plant

items.p: The neelakurinji shrubs on a hillside flower in the same year. Describe one test that could show how the shrubs keep time.
items.a: I could grow cuttings of the shrubs in the same place and see if they flower in the same year as their parents. Or I could record the size of the shrubs each year, to see if they flower when they reach a certain size.
items.why: A strong answer describes a test that gives a clear result, and says what each result would mean.

items.p: Draw flow charts for an annual and for a biennial. Show each stage from seed to seed.
items.a: The annual chart goes from seed to growth, flower, seeds and death within one year. The biennial chart shows year 1 with leaves and a stored root, and year 2 with flower, seeds and death.
items.why: A strong drawing labels the stored root in year 1 of the biennial, and shows the seeds that start the next round.
items.art: A blank page with space for two flow charts with arrows.

items.p: Two plants flowered in 2018, one every 12 years and one every 16 years. When will they flower together again?
items.why: 12 and 16 first meet at 48, because 12 × 4 = 48 and 16 × 3 = 48. 2018 + 48 = 2066.

items.p: Claim: an annual that dies after flowering has failed. Use two facts from this lesson to answer.
items.a: The claim is not fair. An annual puts its food into seeds and leaves thousands of seeds that start the next round. Annuals also cover riverbanks, fields and deserts where perennials cannot hold the ground.
items.why: A strong answer gives two facts, such as the seeds left behind and the places where annuals do well, and reaches a clear verdict.

quiz.p: Pollen lands on a flower. Later, a male cell joins an egg cell inside the flower. What is this stage called?
quiz.why: The joining of a male cell and an egg cell is fertilisation. Choosing pollination means mixing up the carrying of pollen with the joining of cells.

quiz.p: Which stage comes straight after fertilisation?
quiz.why: After fertilisation, the egg cells grow into seeds and the flower around them grows into a fruit. Germination comes later, when a seed starts to grow.

quiz.p: How does a fern make new plants?
quiz.why: Ferns never flower. They make spores, which are single cells. Choosing cones means mixing up ferns with pines.

quiz.p: Which plant makes seeds without any flower or fruit?
quiz.why: A deodar is a conifer, and makes seeds on the scales of cones. Ferns and mosses make spores, and the mango tree has flowers and fruit.

quiz.p: A plant grows leaves and a thick root in year one, flowers in year two and then dies. What is the plant?
quiz.why: A biennial takes two years, and flowers in the second. An annual takes one season, and a perennial lives more than two years.

quiz.p: Which of these plants is a perennial?
quiz.why: A tamarind tree lives for many years. Paddy, mustard and moong live for one season.

quiz.p: Paddy lives about 150 days and first flowers at about day 90. What share of its life passes before the first flower?
quiz.why: 90 ÷ 150 = 3 fifths, which is 60 percent. One third is the share for mustard.

quiz.p: Why do annuals do well in a field that is ploughed every year?
opts: Ploughing clears the ground, and annuals grow quickly from seed
quiz.why: Ploughing clears the plants from the ground. An annual flowers young and leaves seeds before the next clearing, while a perennial loses the years it spent growing.

quiz.p: Why does a young perennial often leave fewer seeds than an annual in the first years?
opts: It spends food on roots and wood, and not on seeds
quiz.why: Food spent on seeds cannot be spent on growing. A perennial grows first and makes seeds for many years afterwards.

quiz.p: A scientist drills a thin core out of a living tree and counts the rings. What does the count tell us?
opts: About how many years old the tree is
How tall the tree will grow
How many leaves the tree has
quiz.why: In places with seasons, a tree adds one ring each year, so the count gives the age. The core does not harm the tree.

quiz.p: In a test that depends on chance, a perennial wins one run. What should you do before you trust this?
opts: Repeat the run several times and look at the average
quiz.why: One run can be lucky. Repeating the run, and using the average, shows the pattern. Stopping after one run mistakes a fluke for a result.

quiz.p: Which is a fair reason to grow perennial crops?
opts: Roots hold the soil all year
Perennial crops always give more grain
Perennial crops grow in one month
quiz.why: Roots in the soil hold it, and the farmer saves the work of sowing. But the farmer must wait some years for the first crop, and some perennial grains give less grain so far.

applications: A farmer who wants carrot or cabbage seed leaves a few plants in the ground for a second year, because these are biennials.
Flower growers light chrysanthemum fields at night, so that the flowers open later and are ready for a festival.
Tree rings in old timber show which years were wet and which were dry. Scientists use them to study the weather of past centuries.
Plant breeders cross rice with wild perennial relatives, to try to make rice that is sown once and harvested for years.
Farmers in Kerala and Karnataka grow banana, pepper and ginger under coconut palms, so that the field gives something every year while the palms grow.
A seed packet states how many days a plant takes from sowing to the first flower. A farmer uses it to plan when to sow.
After clearing a plot of land, gardeners expect annual weeds first and perennial plants later, and plan their work around that order.
Foresters and park staff use growth rates, rings and records to estimate the age of old trees, and decide which trees to protect.
