open_questions.q: How do neelakurinji shrubs count twelve years?
open_questions.why_open: Nobody has found a part of the plant that keeps time. Some scientists think the shrubs flower when they reach a certain size or store of food, and that the weather keeps them in step.

open_questions.q: Do very old trees age, or do they only die from outside causes?
open_questions.why_open: Studies of bristlecone pines and ginkgo trees found no sign of ageing in the growing parts, but other scientists think slow damage builds up. No study has followed a tree for thousands of years.

open_questions.q: Can a perennial grain ever give as much grain as annual rice and wheat?
open_questions.why_open: Perennial rice in China gave yields close to annual rice in tests, but a perennial wheat-like grain still gives much less. The trade-off may be possible to break, or may not.

open_questions.q: How do bamboo plants of one kind flower in the same year, over hundreds of kilometres?
open_questions.why_open: Muli bamboo in Mizoram flowers about every 48 years. Scientists do not yet know what keeps separate clumps in step.

open_questions.q: What was the age of the oldest tree that ever lived?
open_questions.why_open: Trees rot, burn and fall, and their rings are lost. Nobody can count a tree that no longer exists, so there may have been older trees than any we know.

ask_kids: Which plant in our kitchen is an annual, and which is a perennial? How could we find out?
If you could be any plant for one year, would you choose to be an annual or a perennial? Why?
How old do you think the oldest tree near our home is? What clue would you use to guess?
Why do you think chrysanthemums flower in winter, and not in the monsoon?
A mango tree takes five years to flower. Is it worth waiting? What do people do while they wait?
Which plant in a thali has lived the longest before it reached our plate?
If a plant flowers only once in twelve years, how could a family keep the count?
Who planted the trees whose fruit we eat today? Who are we planting for?

jokes.j: Why did the mustard plant finish their life in four months?
jokes.a: It had a very busy schedule.

jokes.j: What did the coconut palm say to the mustard plant?
jokes.a: Slow down. I will be here for eighty years.

jokes.j: Why was the neelakurinji so patient?
jokes.a: It waited twelve years for one party.

jokes.j: What did the annual say to the perennial?
jokes.a: See you next year, in seed form.

jokes.j: Why did the die go to the riverbank?
jokes.a: To clear the ground, one roll at a time.

jokes.j: What did the banana clump say about its oldest stem?
jokes.a: It has done its work, and the children are coming up.

jokes.j: Why did the bristlecone pine never need a birthday cake?
jokes.a: There was no room for 4,800 candles.

jokes.j: What did the scientist say after counting the tree rings?
jokes.a: That tree has seen some years.

jokes.j: Why is the life cycle like a good song?
jokes.a: It always ends where it begins.

maths.problem: In a run of the Bad Year Test in the old grove, the die cleared the ground in 2 of the 12 years. How many seeds did the annual leave, at 5 seeds in a good year?
maths.explain: 12 years minus 2 cleared years leaves 10 good years. 10 × 5 = 50 seeds.
maths.context: In the Bad Year Test, a die decides which years are cleared. The annual makes 5 seeds in each good year.
maths.why_maths: Counting the good years first, and then multiplying, is faster than adding 12 separate years.

maths.problem: A coconut palm first flowers at 8 years of 80. A mango tree first flowers at 5 years of 100. Which tree spends the bigger share of their life before the first flower? By how much?
maths.answer: The coconut palm. It spends 10 percent against 5 percent, which is double.
maths.explain: 8 ÷ 80 = 10 percent. 5 ÷ 100 = 5 percent. 10 is twice 5. So the palm waits for twice the share of its life.
maths.context: In the Stage Lengths activity, you turned lifespans and first flowering ages into shares of the whole life.
maths.why_maths: A share compares plants of very different lifespans on one scale, which the number of years cannot do.

maths.problem: In the Leaf Clock, three stem tips made 5, 7 and 6 new leaf joints in three weeks. The longest stem has 36 leaf joints. Estimate the plant's age in weeks and in months.
maths.explain: The average is (5 + 7 + 6) ÷ 3 = 6 joints in three weeks. 36 ÷ 6 = 6 lots of three weeks. 6 × 3 = 18 weeks, which is about 4 months.
maths.context: In the Leaf Clock, you measure how fast a potted plant makes new leaf joints, and use that rate to estimate the plant's age.
maths.why_maths: The average smooths out the difference between the tips, and dividing by the rate turns a count into a time.

maths.problem: Neelakurinji flowered in 2018 and flowers every 12 years. A girl was born in 2016. How old will she be at the flowerings in 2030, 2042 and 2054?
maths.explain: 2030 − 2016 = 14. 2042 − 2016 = 26. 2054 − 2016 = 38. Each age is 12 more than the one before.
maths.context: In the Rare Flowering Calendar challenge, you mark the years in which a plant flowers and work out your age in each year.
maths.why_maths: A repeating pattern lets you predict a long way ahead, from one known year and one step size.

maths.problem: A bristlecone pine lives about 4,800 years. A mustard plant lives 4 months, so about 3 lifespans in a year. How many mustard lifespans fit into one bristlecone lifespan?
maths.explain: In one year there are 3 mustard lifespans. 4,800 years × 3 = 14,400.
maths.context: This question compares the longest-lived plant in this lesson with one of the shortest, by using a mustard plant's lifespan as a unit of time.
maths.why_maths: Using one lifespan as a unit turns a huge difference into a number that you can imagine.

maths.problem: In a grove with no cleared year in 12 years, the annual leaves 5 seeds a year and the perennial leaves 12 seeds a year after two growing years. Which leaves more, and how many times as many?
maths.answer: The perennial, with 120 seeds against 60. That is twice as many.
maths.explain: The annual: 12 × 5 = 60 seeds. The perennial grows for 2 years, so it makes seeds in 10 years: 10 × 12 = 120. 120 ÷ 60 = 2.
maths.context: In the Bad Year Test, the perennial grows for two years before it makes seeds. This question asks what happens if the ground is never cleared.
maths.why_maths: Working out the best case shows why the perennial can win where the ground is left alone, and why cleared years matter so much.

maths.problem: A field is cleared when a die shows 1 or 2. About how many years in 12 should you expect to be cleared? About how many are good years?
maths.answer: About 4 cleared years and 8 good years.
maths.explain: A 1 or 2 is 2 faces out of 6, which is one third. One third of 12 is 4. So 12 − 4 = 8 good years.
maths.context: In the Fit the Plant to the Field challenge, the die clears a field on some faces. This question asks how many years you should expect to be cleared.
maths.why_maths: Chance cannot tell you one year, but it tells you what to expect over many years, and that lets you compare plans.

quiz: Every flowering plant goes through the same stages in the same order.
The time each stage takes differs a lot, but the order does not.
A fern makes seeds.
A fern makes spores. Spores are single cells, with no young plant and almost no food.
Pollination and fertilisation are the same stage.
Pollination carries the pollen. Fertilisation joins a male cell and an egg cell.
A perennial lives for more than two years.
Mango, coconut and tamarind live for many years.
Banana is a perennial, although it has no wood.
New stems grow from the base, so the clump lives for years.
The biggest tree is always the oldest tree.
The oldest trees counted are small bristlecone pines on dry mountains.
Annuals do well where the ground is often cleared.
A cleared year costs an annual only one season.
A tree adds one ring of wood each year in places with seasons.
Counting the rings gives the age of the tree.
The leaves of a chrysanthemum sense the length of the night.
They send a signal to the buds, and the buds make flowers.
Neelakurinji flowers every year.
The shrubs flower once in about 12 years, all together, and then die.

Fern, moss and pine make no flowers. A rose has flowers.

Floods, fires and ploughing clear plants from the ground. A gentle shower does not.

playtest: Read through step by step as a parent and child in a city flat would use it. The experiments were reasoned through carefully but have not been tried at home. Please treat the expected results as likely and not certain. The Bad Year Test needs a die and a rajma, and can be played anywhere in about 40 minutes. The rules were checked by playing 20,000 simulated runs: in the old grove the perennial leaves more seeds in about 3 runs out of 4, and on the riverbank the annual wins about 9 runs out of 10. A single run can go the other way, which is why the test is repeated three times. The Leaf Clock needs a potted plant with clear stems, such as a money plant, tulsi or curry leaf, and three weeks. If the plant stays dry or the room is cold, no new leaves may open, and the step says what to write then. Same Seed, Different Start Day needs two pots and about 12 weeks. Methi germinates in 3 to 5 days, and flowers about 6 to 9 weeks after sowing in the cool season. Sow between October and February. In the rains the seeds may rot, and in May and June the plants may bolt in the heat. Whatever happens, the child writes down what really happened. Nothing in the lesson needs a garden. The games need paper, a pencil and a rajma. Where Did the Cycle Stop works best with a parent or friend, and Longer or Shorter can be played alone. Facts were checked against published sources on 17 Nov 2026. Confirmed: the neelakurinji and muli bamboo cycles, the bristlecone, ginkgo and perennial rice studies, the Kernza roots and the sequoia age. Corrected: the ginkgo study (trees up to 667 years old) and the dark honey (removed). Softened: the Great Banyan (said to be at least 250 years old), Thimmamma Marrimanu (said to be more than 550 years old), the Anuradhapura peepal (more than 2,200 years, because sources give 288 or 236 BCE), the baobab and talipot ages, and Schulman's 4,600 (a first estimate). The lifespans and first flowering ages in Stage Lengths are typical values and vary by variety and weather. The next flowerings of neelakurinji (about 2030) and muli bamboo (about 2055) are predictions.
